items.title: Portcullis
items.text:
Self-hosted YubiKey authentication gateway for your entire homelab.

Portcullis puts a unified authentication layer in front of all your self-hosted applications. Tap your YubiKey to log in -- one identity, one set of credentials, every app.

items.title: Key Features
items.text:
• WebAuthn (FIDO2) -- Passwordless browser authentication with YubiKey tap
  • mTLS (PIV certificates) -- Client certificate auth for APIs, CLI tools, and service-to-service communication
  • 22+ app templates -- Enable apps like Jellyfin, Nextcloud, Grafana, Immich, and more with one click
  • Hub UI -- Web dashboard to manage apps, view logs, configure settings, and control access
  • Per-app access control -- LLDAP groups determine who can access which apps
  • Single sign-on -- Keycloak-powered OIDC/SAML for apps with native SSO support
  • Forward auth -- Transparent authentication for apps without SSO via oauth2-proxy + group-gate
  • Wildcard TLS -- One wildcard certificate covers all subdomains, with automatic renewal via ACME DNS-01
  • Privacy by design -- Individual subdomain names never appear in Certificate Transparency logs
  • Fully self-hosted -- No external auth providers, no cloud dependencies

items.title: How It Works
items.text:
Traefik sits at the edge as a reverse proxy, terminating TLS and optionally requesting client certificates. Behind it, oauth2-proxy and group-gate enforce authentication and per-app access. Keycloak acts as the identity provider, federating users from LLDAP (a lightweight LDAP directory). Vault PKI issues client certificates (30 days, self-service renewal) for mTLS, and revocation is checked on every request.

Apps choose their auth method: forward-auth for apps without SSO support, native OIDC for apps that speak OpenID Connect, header-auth for apps that trust upstream identity headers, or public for apps that need no authentication.

items.title: Repositories
items.text:
Portcullis is split across four repositories. This site is the documentation for all of them; each repository keeps only a README (and the templates repo its CONTRIBUTING.md).

items.title: Architecture
items.text: Portcullis is a collection of services that work together to provide unified authentication for self-hosted applications. This page describes how the components connect and how authentication flows work.

items.title: Component Roles
items.text: Component Role Traefik Reverse proxy. Terminates TLS (one ACME wildcard cert), routes requests by subdomain, applies middleware chains, optionally requests client certificates. Reads Docker labels through its read-only socket proxy. oauth2-proxy Forward authentication. Redirects unauthenticated users to Keycloak (with per-request acr_values for step-up), and returns identity headers and the access token on success. group-gate Per-request authorization (forward-auth). Checks client-cert revocation, the app's auth policy (acr/amr, mTLS binding), the subdomain's required group and path_groups. Returns 403 or a step-up page. Keycloak Identity provider. WebAuthn (FIDO2), X.509 (YubiKey PIV) login with CRL checks, password, Level-of-Authentication step-up, OIDC/SAML for apps. Federates users from LLDAP. LLDAP Lightweight LDAP directory. Stores users and groups (custom user fields are LLDAP attributes). They are managed in the Hub; directory.<domain> redirects to people.<domain> (LLDAP's own UI has no SSO and is reachable only from the server: portcullis lldap-ui). PostgreSQL Database backend for Keycloak. Vault PKI Private CA in server mode (raft, auto-unseal). Issues client certificates (default 30 days) for YubiKey PIV slots and publishes the CRL. Enrollment UI enroll.<domain>: admins enroll WebAuthn and PIV certificates; any user renews their own certificate at /self. Signs CSRs through a least-privilege Vault AppRole. Hub Two listeners: hub.<domain> (admins only): app catalog, runs each enabled app instance as its own compose project, registers Keycloak clients, writes the policy file v5 (keyed by full hostname) and user-attributes.json, delivers app settings (Settings Delivery), reports drift, manages enrolled domains. people.<domain> (any signed-in user): Users & Groups (People, Groups, Org chart, Import) with per-request permission checks (admins, or delegated edit_details / invite / remove permissions), and My apps (each person's own app settings). Domains service Manages enrolled extra domains: creates DNS records, obtains wildcard certificates via ACME DNS-01, serves them to Traefik over its HTTP provider. Credentials stored encrypted at rest (age). See Security & Hardening. forward-auth-ext Second oauth2-proxy for extra-domain hosts. Relative callback /oauth2/callback, host-only cookie __Host-portcullis_ext. Shares the Keycloak client with forward-auth. See Hub Management. Monitoring (optional) Compose profile monitoring: Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana at metrics.<domain> (lldap_admin), blackbox and textfile exporters. See Monitoring. mcp-gate Terminates every MCP request of people's AI clients (mcp.<domain>, each app's /mcp endpoint, hub.<domain>/mcp, people.<domain>/mcp): checks the Keycloak token for exactly that resource, the person's population on every request, tool policy, limits and confirmations, logs every call, and forwards it to the app's companion as the person, never with their token. See AI support and AI support flow. Socket proxies socket-proxy-traefik (read-only) and socket-proxy-hub (what compose needs): the only containers that mount the Docker socket. See Security & Hardening.

items.title: Repository Structure
items.text:
Portcullis is organized as four separate repositories, each with a distinct responsibility. Their interfaces are defined in Integration Contracts.

  • Core repo (porelli/portcullis) -- docker-compose.yml for all core services, the ./portcullis admin CLI (libraries in scripts/lib/), group-gate (group-gate/), the enrollment UI (enroll/), Traefik dynamic configuration (traefik/), Vault configuration (vault/) and the Keycloak realm export. This is the only repo you need to clone to deploy Portcullis.

  • Hub repo (porelli/portcullis-hub) -- The management web UI, published as a signed container image at ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub (selected with HUB_IMAGE).

  • Templates repo (porelli/portcullis-templates) -- The app templates (<app-id>/manifest.yaml + compose.yml), the manifest JSON Schema and the template validator. The Hub clones it on first startup as the default template source. Accepts outside contributions.

  • Docs repo (porelli/portcullis-docs) -- This documentation site, built with Zensical. App catalog pages are generated from the template manifests.

items.title: Authentication Flows
items.text: Portcullis supports four authentication methods. Each app declares its method in its manifest.yaml.

items.title: Forward Auth (oauth2-proxy + group-gate)
items.text:
Used by apps that have no native SSO support (Pi-hole, DokuWiki, Scrutiny, etc.). Traefik delegates authentication to oauth2-proxy and authorization to group-gate before the request reaches the app. The router's middleware chain is client-headers@file,portcullis-auth@docker,portcullis-groups@docker,security-headers@file; client-headers@file must come first so group-gate sees the client certificate (for revocation and the mTLS binding).

If the session does not satisfy the app's access policy, group-gate answers with a 403 step-up page that redirects to https://auth.<domain>/oauth2/start?acr_values=<needed>&prompt=login&rd=https://<app>/, and Keycloak prompts for the missing factor. (oauth2-proxy only serves /oauth2/* on auth.<domain>: a host-less router would get Traefik's default TLS options and be refused with 421 on every app host.)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant T as Traefik
    participant O as oauth2-proxy
    participant G as group-gate
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant A as App

    U->>T: GET https://pihole.example.com
    T->>O: Forward auth check
    O-->>T: 401 (no session)
    T-->>U: 302 Redirect to oauth2-proxy /sign_in
    U->>O: Follow redirect
    O-->>U: 302 Redirect to Keycloak
    U->>K: Keycloak login (WebAuthn / YubiKey tap)
    K-->>U: 302 Redirect to oauth2-proxy /callback
    U->>O: Callback with auth code
    O->>K: Exchange code for tokens
    K-->>O: ID token + access token (includes groups)
    O-->>U: Set session cookie, redirect to app
    U->>T: GET https://pihole.example.com (with cookie)
    T->>O: Forward auth check
    O-->>T: 200 OK (X-Auth-Request-*, access token)
    T->>G: Check (host, groups, access token, URI, client cert info)
    Note over G: revocation, policy (acr/amr), group users_pihole, path_groups
    G-->>T: 200 OK (X-Forwarded-User, X-Auth-Request-Groups)
    T->>A: Forward request
    A-->>U: App response

items.title: Native OIDC
items.text:
Used by apps with built-in OpenID Connect support (Jellyfin, Immich, Vaultwarden, Nextcloud, etc.). The app redirects to Keycloak directly, without oauth2-proxy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant T as Traefik
    participant A as App
    participant K as Keycloak

    U->>T: GET https://photos.example.com
    T->>A: Forward request
    A-->>U: 302 Redirect to Keycloak authorize endpoint
    U->>K: Keycloak login (WebAuthn / YubiKey tap)
    K-->>U: 302 Redirect to app callback
    U->>T: GET https://photos.example.com/callback?code=...
    T->>A: Forward request
    A->>K: Exchange code for tokens
    K-->>A: ID token + access token
    A-->>U: Set session, app response

items.title: Header Auth
items.text:
Used by apps that accept a trusted identity header from the reverse proxy (Grafana, Kanboard, Firefly III, Guacamole, CloudBeaver). The user authenticates via forward auth, and the app reads X-Forwarded-User (the LLDAP username, set by group-gate; the email travels separately in X-Forwarded-Email). The app accepts that header only from Traefik's fixed IP, so other containers on portcullis-proxy cannot impersonate users.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant T as Traefik
    participant O as oauth2-proxy
    participant G as group-gate
    participant A as App

    U->>T: GET https://grafana.example.com
    Note over T,O: Forward auth (same as above)
    T->>O: Forward auth check
    O-->>T: 200 OK
    T->>G: Group check
    G-->>T: 200 OK (X-Forwarded-User: alice)
    T->>A: Request from PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP with X-Forwarded-User
    A-->>U: App logs in alice automatically

items.title: mTLS (Client Certificate)
items.text:
When mTLS is enabled, the browser presents the X.509 certificate stored in the YubiKey's PIV slot during the TLS handshake. Traefik verifies it against the Portcullis CA chain, but does not check revocation; that happens in group-gate and Keycloak.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User + YubiKey
    participant T as Traefik
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant G as group-gate
    participant A as App

    U->>T: TLS handshake (client cert)
    T->>T: Verify chain against certs/ca-chain.crt
    U->>T: GET https://auth.example.com/... (login)
    T->>K: via portcullis-auth, X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert (PEM)
    Note over K: trusts the header only from Traefik's IP,<br/>re-validates chain + EKU, checks Vault CRL (fail closed)
    K-->>U: Session with amr=mtls (LoA 3)
    U->>T: GET https://app.example.com (cookie + client cert)
    T->>G: forward-auth with X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info
    Note over G: serial not revoked? policy needs mtls only?<br/>then cert CN must equal preferred_username
    G-->>T: 200 OK
    T->>A: Forward request

Routers on the protected tier without forward-auth (mtls-method apps) rely on the TLS handshake alone: there the certificate works until it expires. See TLS & mTLS.

items.title: TLS Tiers
items.text:
Traefik is configured with three TLS option sets. Each app chooses its tier based on its security requirements.

Tier Traefik TLS Option Client Cert Behavior Use Case protected RequireAndVerifyClientCert Required -- TLS handshake fails without a valid cert Highest security apps (mtls-method apps) authaware VerifyClientCertIfGiven Optional -- verified if present, WebAuthn fallback if not Most apps (default for forward-auth and OIDC apps) public NoClientCert Not requested Public-facing apps, apps that manage their own auth

When MTLS_ENABLED=false in .env, all three tiers behave like public -- no client certificates are requested for any app. Routers that relied on protected alone become unauthenticated.

For apps the Hub sets the tier from the app's access policy, not from the template (see Authentication Policies).

items.title: Network Topology
items.text:
Traefik is the only service exposed to the internet (ports 80 and 443). It is attached to every network it has to reach; nothing else bridges them.

  • portcullis -- Core services: Keycloak, LLDAP, Vault, PostgreSQL, oauth2-proxy, group-gate, Hub, enroll. Apps are not on it and cannot reach these services directly.
  • portcullis-proxy -- Traefik and app frontend services; Traefik's docker provider routes over it. Fixed subnet (PORTCULLIS_PROXY_SUBNET, default 172.31.250.0/24), Traefik always at PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP (default 172.31.250.2), other containers from PORTCULLIS_PROXY_IP_RANGE (which excludes Traefik's IP). Header-auth apps trust identity headers only from Traefik's address.
  • portcullis-auth -- Internal network with only Traefik (fixed PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP, default 172.31.251.2) and Keycloak. Keycloak accepts proxy headers -- including the forwarded client certificate for X.509 login -- only from that address.
  • portcullis-mcp -- Internal network with only mcp-gate, Keycloak and the Hub (fixed addresses): the gate fetches Keycloak's keys and calls the Hub's MCP listener here. The gate also sits on portcullis-proxy at PORTCULLIS_MCP_GATE_IP (default 172.31.250.3), where Traefik routes MCP requests to it and it reaches the app companions.
  • socket-proxy-traefik, socket-proxy-hub -- Internal networks, each shared by one client and its Docker socket proxy.
  • Per-app networks -- Each app's compose project (portcullis-<app-id>) has its own default network. Internal services (databases, caches, workers) live only there, isolated from all other apps.

Frontend services join both default and portcullis-proxy; internal services only default.

Security & Hardening lists every network's members and addressing rules.

Native OIDC apps that need to reach Keycloak do so over HTTPS via the public URL (https://auth.<domain>), not via the internal network.

DNS is configured as a wildcard record (*.portcullis.example.com), so all subdomains resolve to the same server IP. Traefik routes each subdomain to the correct container based on Docker labels.

items.title: Custom Attributes Flow
items.text:
Custom user fields (department, office, manager, etc.) defined in the Hub flow to apps in two ways:

flowchart LR
    LLDAP[(LLDAP<br/>custom attributes)]
    Hub[Hub<br/>evaluates rules,<br/>reads attributes]
    UAFile[user-attributes.json<br/>hub_data volume]
    GG[group-gate]
    App1[Forward-auth /<br/>Header-auth Apps]
    KC[Keycloak<br/>LDAP mappers]
    Scope[portcullis-attributes<br/>client scope]
    App2[Native OIDC Apps]

    LLDAP -->|GraphQL| Hub
    Hub -->|writes atomically| UAFile
    Hub -->|creates mappers| KC
    UAFile -->|reads on every request| GG
    GG -->|X-Forwarded-Attr-*<br/>percent-encoded, ', ' joined| App1
    KC -->|LDAP sync| LLDAP
    KC -->|attr_<field> claims| Scope
    Scope -->|in ID token| App2

items.title: For Forward-Auth and Header-Auth Apps
items.text:
1. LLDAP: stores users and custom attributes (created by the Hub as non-user-editable LLDAP user attributes).
  2. Hub: reads field values via GraphQL, evaluates rules, writes user-attributes.json (only fields with share_with_apps: true) atomically with the policy file.
  3. group-gate: reads user-attributes.json on every request. On allow, returns X-Forwarded-Attr-<Header-Name> headers. Values are percent-encoded (% → %25, , → %2C), joined with ,, limited to 1 KB per value (before encoding).
  4. Traefik: forwards these headers to the app (the portcullis-groups middleware uses authResponseHeadersRegex: ^X-Forwarded-Attr-). Client copies are stripped by the forwardAuth regex.
  5. App: receives the headers. Apps must percent-decode each value after splitting on ,.

items.title: For Native OIDC Apps
items.text:
1. LLDAP: stores users and custom attributes.
  2. Hub: on every field change (create, update, delete, or share_with_apps toggle), syncs Keycloak LDAP attribute mappers on the portcullis-attributes client scope via the Keycloak admin API. Each shared field gets:
    • an LDAP attribute mapper: portcullis-attr-<field> (reads <field> from LDAP)
    • a protocol mapper: attr_<field> claim (user attribute <field> → claim attr_<field> in ID token, access token, userinfo)
  3. Keycloak: syncs users from LLDAP via LDAP federation (periodic and manual sync). The mappers read field values from LDAP.
  4. App: receives attr_<field> claims in the ID token (no percent-encoding; multi-valued fields are JSON arrays).

The Hub attaches the portcullis-attributes client scope as a default scope to every client it creates. On reconcile, it re-attaches missing mappers.

items.title: Settings Delivery
items.text:
App settings (Hub → App settings, contracts §13) are declared by the template and delivered by the Hub. The Hub stores canonical values (bytes, seconds, typed JSON) in state.yaml and secrets in a separate 0600 store, then works out what each app should see and hands it over in the form the template asked for.

flowchart LR
    Admin[Admin<br/>settings panel]
    Person[Person<br/>My apps]
    Dir[(LLDAP<br/>groups, members)]
    Hub[Hub delivery engine<br/>one run per instance]
    Env[.env<br/>read at start]
    File[data files<br/>appfiles/id/name]
    Hook[hooks<br/>docker exec, JSON on stdin]
    Attr[(LLDAP setting attributes<br/>ps-hash)]
    KC[Keycloak mappers]
    UA[user-attributes.json<br/>hosts]
    GG[group-gate]
    App[App]

    Admin -->|save| Hub
    Person -->|own value| Hub
    Dir -->|membership snapshot| Hub
    Hub --> Env --> App
    Hub --> File -->|read-only mount| App
    Hub --> Hook --> App
    Hub --> Attr --> KC -->|claims at sign-in| App
    Hub --> UA --> GG -->|X-Forwarded-Attr-* per host| App

One delivery run, per instance and never two at once:

  1. Snapshot. The Hub reads the directory once (members, group ids, account ids) and works out the population: who has access to the instance. Group rows and records count only when their group still has the LLDAP id they were saved with.
  2. Resolve. Per-person options get one value per person (max, min, priority, …); values people entered are kept for people still in the population whose account still matches.
  3. Compare. Each unit's desired output (the env, each data file, each claim attribute, the headers, each hook's input) is compared with what was last delivered (delivered.json: hashes only, never values). Unchanged units are skipped.
  4. Deliver, in order: data files, then claims (an LLDAP attribute per option, written per person, and a mapper on the instance's Keycloak client), then headers (published with the policy file), then hooks, then the strongest effect: nothing, one reload or one restart (in the background).
  5. Record the outcome per unit; the panel's Deliveries strip shows it.

If the settings change during a run, the stale run stops at its next write (superseded) and a new run starts with the newest state. If the directory is unavailable, units that need people keep their last delivery. A disabled instance gets nothing; a busy one (another operation running) is retried shortly. Membership changes are debounced 60 seconds per instance, so a batch of joins gives one restart. On start, data files are written before the containers are created, and start hooks run after a successful start.

Each delivery fails closed: a value that can't be rendered for a claim or header is left out (the person gets none, never someone else's or a default), and a stale claim value is never kept in a token mapper.

items.title: File Sharing (Samba and Time Machine)
items.text:
The Samba and Time Machine templates serve SMB3 with a password of each person's own (operator guide, contracts §13.16–§13.17). They have no web page and no Traefik router. The Hub knows nothing about Samba: it implements two generic option types, person_secret (a password per person) and person_id (a uid per person), plus hooks, tsv data files and hook reports. Everything Samba-specific is in the templates' manifests and their converge script, portcullis-sync.

flowchart TB
    Person[Person on My apps<br/>people.domain]
    KC[Keycloak<br/>portcullis-fresh-auth client]
    Hub[Hub]
    Secrets[(hub_secrets volume<br/>10001:10001, mode 0700)]
    People[people.tsv data file<br/>uids, shares, groups]
    LLDAP[(LLDAP<br/>users, groups)]
    App[Samba / Time Machine container<br/>portcullis-sync + smbd]

    Person -->|popup: fresh hardware sign-in, PKCE| KC
    Person -->|code, verifier, nonce| Hub
    Hub -->|code exchange, ID token check| KC
    Hub -->|NT hash file per person| Secrets
    Hub -->|delivery engine| People
    LLDAP -->|membership snapshot| Hub
    Secrets -.->|subpath, read-only<br/>/portcullis/secrets| App
    People -.->|read-only<br/>/portcullis/data| App
    Hub -->|sync hook: docker exec,<br/>HookInput on stdin| App
    App -->|PORTCULLIS-REPORT line| Hub

items.title: hub_secrets volume
items.text:
• Core declares the volume hub_secrets (portcullis_hub_secrets), mounts it into the Hub at /secrets (HUB_SECRETS_DIR), and sets its root to 10001:10001, mode 0700 (the Hub's uid) on every init, up, upgrade and restore.
  • The Hub checks the owner and mode at start. If they are wrong, the credential routes answer 503 and every instance with a person_secret option refuses to start, naming the reason.
  • Contents: one directory per instance and option, <instance>/<key>/ (0700). Each holds one <username>.nt per active password (0600, owner 10001): the uppercase hex of MD4 over the UTF-16LE encoding of the password, 32 characters and a newline. The volume also holds .epoch (below).
  • Mounts: the Hub's override mounts only that instance's and option's directory, read-only, as a volume subpath at /portcullis/secrets in the template's one service. A container never sees another instance's hashes. Before every up the Hub checks that nothing else mounts the volume.
  • Backups: the volume is never backed up. A core restore empties it (Backups).

items.title: Creating a password
items.text:
1. On My apps the person clicks Create password. The page opens Keycloak's portcullis-fresh-auth client in a popup (PKCE S256, prompt=login, max_age=0, acr_values=hwk), so they sign in again with their hardware key.
  2. The popup hands the code back to the page, which posts the code, the PKCE verifier and the nonce to the Hub. The Hub exchanges the code with Keycloak itself and checks the ID token: the sign-in is at most 300 s old, amr contains hwk or mtls (never file), the nonce matches, aud / azp is the client, and preferred_username is the caller.
  3. The Hub draws 24 characters from a 54-character alphabet with crypto/rand. It shows them as 6 groups of 4 joined by -: 29 characters, dashes included. The Hub computes the NT hash itself.
  4. Under the Hub's lock, it writes the hash file, rotates the secrets epoch, and saves the metadata (id, version, uuid, dates; never the hash) to state.yaml. Then it writes the audit.
  5. The password goes into the one answer (Cache-Control: no-store) and the buffer is zeroed. It never appears anywhere else: not in logs, the audit, hook input or output, or a backup.
  6. An immediate credential_change delivery runs the app's hook. A regenerate also removes the old hash: it is applied like a revocation (below), so the old password stops working even when the hook is skipped or fails.

Ids: each person gets a uid from the Hub-wide pool posix_uid, 20000–59999. A uid is allocated once, keyed by username and LLDAP uuid, and never reused. An account that is deleted and created again gets a new uid, so it never owns the former account's files.

items.title: People file and the sync hook
items.text:
The people file is an ordinary settings data file (Settings Delivery) in tsv format, read-only at /portcullis/data/people.tsv. It holds each person's uid, the connect address and the Bonjour switch. For Samba it also holds the share names and the reader and writer groups, expanded to their members. For Time Machine it holds the share prefix and each person's size limit. The delivery engine renders it like any data file. It is written again when people join or leave, when a setting changes, and on every start. A change to it runs the hook (on_membership_change: hook).

The hook sync (portcullis-sync, timeout 60 s) runs on start, settings_change, membership_change and credential_change. Docker exec gives it the full desired state on stdin as JSON (the HookInput), never a diff:

  • trigger comes first;
  • then the data-file document;
  • then credentials: for each person with an active password, its id and version, never a hash.

The script reads the hashes from its own read-only mount. It converges, idempotently and under its own lock:

  1. the Unix accounts (each person's Hub uid; every other account in its range is removed);
  2. the passdb, on tmpfs;
  3. the whole smb.conf, which testparm must show exactly as hardened.

It then ends the open sessions of people whose account went, whose hash changed, or whose shares shrank or went from write to read.

Any failure after a change has started is fail-closed: the script stops smbd and writes a down marker, which the healthcheck and smbd's run script refuse until a run succeeds. The script prints one PORTCULLIS-REPORT line (below 60 KiB). The line holds:

  • former accounts' folders;
  • wrong owners;
  • refused share and user names;
  • the per-person folder sizes.

A detached background job measures the sizes, and every hook run reports the last ones it cached. The Hub keeps the last report for the File sharing tab and the doctor. A report never drives revocation.

items.title: Revocation
items.text:
A password is revoked when its holder leaves the instance's access group, is deleted (or deleted and created again), revokes it on My apps, or an admin revokes it on the File sharing tab. The Hub runs one holder check for every trigger:

  • Hub-made changes (member removal, user or group deletion) and the rule evaluator's removals: the check runs at once, with no debounce.
  • Changes made directly in LLDAP: the check runs on the evaluator's 60 s tick. The same tick also compares the share readers and writers with the last delivered people file. A removal delivers at once, and the hook ends the sessions of people whose shares shrank.

Every revocation is applied the same way, outside the delivery engine:

  1. Under the Hub's lock, the hash file and the active metadata go (the epoch is rotated). Then the audit is written.
  2. No running container: done. The next start's converge has no account for them.
  3. Otherwise the Hub runs the credential_change hooks with a freshly built HookInput. It holds the instance's delivery lock (taken within 2 s) and gives each exec at most 8 s.
  4. Anything else is handled by the kill path. That covers: no hook run, the lock not obtained, a skip, a failure, a timeout, or a hash file that may remain. The Hub kills the project (compose down) and starts it again in the background, so no old session survives. A hash file that may remain also makes the Hub refuse to start file-sharing instances until a secrets reconcile succeeds.

Every lifecycle down of the instance (backup, restore, delete, restart, disable) waits once, at most 10 s, for the delivery lock, so a revocation hook in flight finishes; then it goes on. A restart's start step then waits for the delivery lock without a time limit. Measured in the core e2e-filesharing CI job (three runs, plus one more), from the change until the session was gone and a new login was refused:

  • a removal through the Hub took 0.8–0.9 s;
  • a removal directly in LLDAP took 3.4–51.8 s (it waits for the 60 s tick);
  • a writer demoted to reader took 3.5–3.6 s.

See Measured revocation times.

items.title: Secrets epoch and restores
items.text:
The Hub writes a random epoch (16 random bytes, hex) both into state.yaml and into <secrets>/.epoch. It rotates the epoch on every credential mutation: create, regenerate, revoke and void. At boot, and before every credentials delivery unit, it compares the two.

On a mismatch, every credential of every instance is voided (reason: restore) and the volume is emptied. A mismatch comes from a core restore, an older state.yaml next to a newer volume, or a crash between the two writes. Every uid pool also advances by 1000, so a pool restored from an older state.yaml never hands out a uid that files on disk may carry. An instance restore voids that instance's credentials only. In both cases, My apps shows "Your password was reset by a restore on ; create a new one."

items.title: Shared folders and the doctor
items.text:
A shared folder is a host directory several app instances use. The Hub gives it one group (a gid from 60000–60999, or an adopted one), mounts it into each app (read-only for readers), adds the gid to the app's groups, and keeps the files' ownership consistent: the folder's group, setgid directories and default ACLs, so whatever uid and umask an app writes with, the others can use the result. The rules are contracts §13.15 and §14.

flowchart LR
    Admin[Admin<br/>Shared folders / Doctor]
    Hub[Hub]
    Proxy[socket-proxy-hub]
    Fixer[fixer helper<br/>Hub image, uid 0,<br/>mode's capabilities only,<br/>no network]
    Folder[(host folder<br/>/srv/media)]
    Snap[(permissions snapshots<br/>hub_data)]
    Apps[App instances]

    Admin -->|preview, apply| Hub
    Hub -->|Docker API| Proxy -->|start / remove| Fixer
    Fixer -->|probe, scan, apply, restore| Folder
    Fixer -->|snapshot| Snap
    Hub -->|stop, regenerate, start| Apps
    Apps -->|bind mount + group| Folder

The Hub never touches host files itself and has no host shell. Every change goes through a short-lived fixer helper (the Hub's own image, started through the Hub's socket proxy, one bind mount of the folder) and through one sequence: preview (nothing changes) → stop the affected apps → permissions snapshot → apply exactly the planned entries → verify → save the settings → start the apps. Undo restores the snapshot the same way. See Security & Hardening for the helper's limits.

The doctor reads the whole setup (state, templates, overrides, ports, settings, group membership, cached disk scans, and the groups of the processes running in each app's containers) and reports findings with their severity and the fix it offers: one-click fixes go through the same previewed operations, risky ones are explained, and it never changes anything by itself. It also judges ports templates mark LAN only against the admin's local networks.

items.title: AI Support Flow
items.text:
People's AI clients (Claude, Claude Code, an AI page) reach apps through mcp-gate, as the person (AI support):

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as AI client
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant G as mcp-gate
    participant H as Hub
    participant A as App companion
    C->>G: POST https://gitea.<d>/mcp (no token)
    G-->>C: 401, resource metadata (RFC 9728)
    C->>K: authorize (PKCE, scope mcp:gitea.gitea), passkey, consent
    K-->>C: access token (aud = https://gitea.<d>/mcp)
    C->>G: tools/call + Bearer token
    G->>G: signature, issuer, audience, scope, client, LoA,<br/>population now, tool policy, limits
    alt no app credential yet (app_token)
        G->>H: POST /internal/credentials (gate secret)
        H->>A: mint hook (in the app's container)
        H-->>G: credential, encrypted to the gate
    end
    alt confirm tool
        G->>H: POST /internal/confirmations
        G-->>C: "needs your confirmation": people.<d>/confirm/<id>
        Note over C,H: the person approves with a passkey, the AI retries
    end
    G->>A: the call, with the person's credential (never the token)
    A-->>G: result
    G->>G: one access-log line
    G-->>C: result
  • One resource per token. Each MCP endpoint is its own OAuth resource; the Hub creates a Keycloak scope per resource whose audience mapper puts exactly that URL in aud. A token for one app works at no other.
  • The Hub owns the Keycloak AI clients and mcp:* scopes, writes the gate's files (mcp-gate.json: resources, populations, tool policy; mcp-credentials.json: per-person credentials encrypted to the gate), runs the companions' mint and revoke hooks, serves the confirmation pages and the Portcullis MCP on its third listener (:8890, reachable only with the gate secret).
  • All my apps (mcp.<d>/mcp) is served by the gate itself: it lists the tools of every companion the person can use (<instance>__<tool>) plus the people tools (portcullis__<tool>), and routes each call as if it came directly, with every per-app rule.
  • Leaving an app's population refuses the person at their next request; the Hub revokes their app credentials, and once they can use no AI resource at all, their Keycloak consents and offline sessions.

items.title: Expiry Flow
items.text:
Temporary group memberships (manual memberships with expiry, or exceptions with expiry in rule-based groups) are enforced strictly, even while the Hub is down.

flowchart TD
    Admin[Admin sets expiry<br/>or creates exception<br/>with expiry]
    Hub[Hub writes entry<br/>to policy file<br/>expiring array]
    LLDAP[(LLDAP<br/>membership<br/>still present)]
    Eval[Hub evaluator<br/>runs ≤ 60s]
    Check{now >= at?}
    GG[group-gate<br/>reads policy file<br/>on every request]
    Remove[Hub removes<br/>from LLDAP,<br/>revokes Keycloak<br/>sessions]
    Grace[Hub keeps entry<br/>+ 10 min grace]
    Clear[Hub clears<br/>grace entry]

    Admin --> Hub
    Hub -->|immediately| LLDAP
    Hub -->|immediately| GG
    Eval --> Check
    Check -->|not yet| GG
    Check -->|yes| Remove
    Remove --> Grace
    Grace -->|on regrant| Clear
    GG -->|treats as absent<br/>withholds token| App[App denied]
    Remove -->|oauth2-proxy refresh 1m| App2[OIDC apps lose<br/>access within ~1 min]
  1. Admin sets an expiry (date/time) on a membership or exception in the Hub.
  2. Hub writes the entry to the policy file's expiring array immediately: {"user": "<username>", "group": "<group>", "at": "<RFC 3339 UTC timestamp>"}. The entry stays in LLDAP.
  3. group-gate reads the policy file on every request. When now >= at, it treats the membership as absent, regardless of what the user's token says. It also withholds Authorization and X-Forwarded-Access-Token for that request.
  4. Forward-auth apps: denied immediately (403 from group-gate).
  5. Native OIDC apps: the token still has the group claim until the next Keycloak token refresh.
  6. Hub evaluator runs at least every 60 seconds and on changes. When it finds an expired entry, it:
    • removes the membership from LLDAP,
    • revokes the user's Keycloak sessions (so OIDC apps lose access at their next token refresh; oauth2-proxy cookie refresh is 1 minute, so this happens within ~1 minute),
    • keeps the expiring entry (plus a 10-minute grace period) until the membership is actually removed and the grace ends, or until regrant (admin re-adds, exception include, rule change adds them back).

The grace period ensures enforcement stays strict even if the Hub is restarted or LLDAP removal fails: group-gate keeps denying based on the policy file until the Hub successfully removes the entry and clears it.

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_ai-chat Subdomain ai

Auth Notes

LibreChat 0.8.8 signs people in through Keycloak (OpenID only: no password login, no local sign-up, no password reset). Only members of users_ai-chat get in: the Hub's Keycloak access role refuses everyone else, and LibreChat itself requires the access group in the ID token's groups claim. Accounts are keyed on the token's sub; the name shown is the LLDAP username. Nobody is a LibreChat administrator (OpenID accounts are plain users), and the configuration comes only from the Hub. The AI side: one MCP server, "All my apps" (https://mcp./mcp), reached with each person's own OAuth token of the instance's ai-chat-mcp client (scope mcp:all): each person connects once and consents in Keycloak; nobody can add other MCP servers. Nothing a person does makes the server fetch a URL they chose: agents have no actions (OpenAPI calls), web search, code interpreter, file search or OCR, and of LibreChat's built-in tools only the calculator is offered. Conversations can't be shared (no shared links, public or not), and a link can't submit a prompt by itself. Models: the providers selected on the instance's AI tab (Hub Settings → AI), each shown under its label. Everyone who can open the instance can use every provider selected for it, and what they send, and what their apps return, goes to that provider; give a group other providers with another ai-chat instance and its own access group. Kinds: OpenAI-compatible servers and LiteLLM, OpenAI, Anthropic (LibreChat's native Messages API client), Google (Gemini through Google's OpenAI-compatible API, https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai unless the provider sets its own base URL) and Azure OpenAI deployment groups. AWS Bedrock isn't offered: LibreChat takes Bedrock credentials only from its own fixed variables, never as a configuration reference. Keys are never written to a file: librechat.yaml holds ${VAR} references LibreChat expands from its environment. A provider with per-person keys asks each person for their own key (not possible for Azure OpenAI: the instance refuses to start). A provider whose key isn't set yet is left out until it is. Upgrades: LibreChat's api and config services share one image; MongoDB stays on 7.0 (MongoDB 8 refuses Linux kernels 6.19 to 7.0.13) and its majors and Meilisearch minors move by hand with LibreChat's own compose file (the search index is rebuilt from MongoDB).

CloudBeaver's reverseProxy auth provider logs users in from X-Forwarded-User (the immutable LLDAP username; the provider has no email header) and trusts team/role headers from any peer with no allowlist, so CloudBeaver is kept off portcullis-proxy behind a small nginx gate (cloudbeaver-gate) that rejects (403) X-Forwarded-User or X-Forwarded-Email from anything but Traefik (PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP) and strips the X-User/X-Team/X-Role/X-Role-TE/name and X-Forwarded-Email headers. Accounts created when the header carried the email are named after it; rename them to the LLDAP username in CloudBeaver's admin UI. Roles and connections are managed in CloudBeaver. The server is configured automatically at first start (CB_SERVER_* / CB_ADMIN_*), so nobody gets the initial-configuration wizard; its local administrator cbadmin- (password CLOUDBEAVER_ADMIN_PASSWORD, both generated per instance) is break-glass only. reverseProxy logs a user in as the CloudBeaver account named like X-Forwarded-User, so the administrator's name is per instance and non-guessable, and cloudbeaver-gate refuses (403) any X-Forwarded-User starting with "cbadmin" (case-insensitive), so no LLDAP user can become the local administrator. Before every start, cloudbeaver-config (a one-shot, JSON-aware patch of workspace/.data/.cloudbeaver.runtime.conf) re-enables the reverseProxy provider with X-Forwarded-User, and CloudBeaver doesn't start if that fails. Anonymous access is off (fail closed); on the first start cloudbeaver-config seeds the runtime config before the automatic configuration runs, so users sign in by X-Forwarded-User from the start. cloudbeaver-gate is healthy only while CloudBeaver reports itself configured (no setup wizard) with anonymous access off; Traefik routes no unhealthy container, so a failed automatic configuration is never served.

items.title: 📝 DokuWiki
items.text:
Simple, file-based wiki — no database required, easy backups

Category: productivity Tags: wiki, docs, knowledge-base, file-based Website: https://www.dokuwiki.org/ Source: https://github.com/dokuwiki/dokuwiki

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_dokuwiki Admin Group admin_dokuwiki Subdomain dokuwiki

Auth Notes

Native OIDC through the oauth + oauthgeneric plugins (https://www.dokuwiki.org/plugin:oauth, https://www.dokuwiki.org/plugin:oauthgeneric; maintained by CosmoCode, DokuWiki's authors), vendored in the template (dokuwiki/plugins, see VENDORED; no download at start) and configured by init.sh at every start (conf/local.protected.php, which the admin UI can't override). Fail closed: init.sh first locks the wiki down (install.php deleted, no auth backend so DokuWiki grants nothing, login disabled) and only its last step writes the OIDC configuration, so a failed start leaves a wiki that nobody can read or sign in to (the container log says why). One Portcullis login: the login page only offers the Portcullis button. Why not header auth: the header plugins in the DokuWiki repository (authserversso, genericsso, authremoteuser, authenvvars) read a server variable from any client, have no proxy allowlist, map no groups and are barely maintained (https://www.dokuwiki.org/plugins?pluginsort=p&plugintype=128). Identity: the oauth plugin finds accounts by their email, and LLDAP emails are user-editable, so init.sh maps the plugin's mail field to preferred_username (the immutable LLDAP username) and disables profile edits; the account name is the username too. DokuWiki therefore has no real email addresses (no subscription mails). Rights: anonymous visitors get nothing (ACL "* @ALL 0", re-applied at every start together with "* @users_dokuwiki 8"; rules for @ALL, @user and @generic are replaced, others kept), members of users_dokuwiki read, edit and upload, and members of admin_dokuwiki are superusers. Groups follow the groups claim at each login (overwrite-groups); a realm user outside access_group can't sign in (Keycloak denies it, see below) and would get no rights anyway. Removing a user from the groups takes effect at their next login. Break-glass: there is no password form (singleService); with shell access, add a local user with bin/plugin.php usermanager and set singleService to 0 in conf/local.protected.php (until the next restart). Hostname: init.sh writes baseurl from the instance's hostname at every start, so a hostname change only needs a restart. install.php is deleted at every start (the configuration is written by init.sh). Existing local accounts keep their pages but can't sign in with a password; an LLDAP user whose name is taken by a local account gets a numbered account name (e.g. admin1). Sign-in is restricted to access_group in Keycloak (keycloak_access_role, contract §8 Access role): only access_group members can sign in, so a member of admin_group who is not also in access_group is denied — put the wiki's admins in both groups.

items.title: 📟 ESPHome
items.text:
ESPHome Device Builder — write, compile and flash ESP32/ESP8266 firmware from YAML

Category: home-automation Tags: home-automation, esphome, iot, firmware, esp32, smart-home Website: https://esphome.io/ Source: https://github.com/esphome/esphome

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method forward-auth SSO No Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_esphome Admin Group admin_esphome Subdomain esphome

Auth Notes

ESPHome 2026.10's dashboard is ESPHome Device Builder (esphome-device-builder 1.25.0 in the image; ESPHome removed its legacy dashboard in 2026.7). It has no user system: its only login is an optional single username/password (ESPHOME_USERNAME / ESPHOME_PASSWORD), and without one every peer that reaches port 6052 is fully trusted. Here it runs without that password: forward-auth + group-gate on the whole host is the sign-in, and every member of the access group can do everything (edit device YAML and secrets.yaml, which hold Wi-Fi passwords and API keys, compile, flash). The dashboard is on the instance's private network only; the gate in front of it (nginx, the only container on portcullis-proxy) answers Traefik's address alone, so no other container can reach the dashboard unauthenticated. The gate never forwards the Portcullis session to the dashboard (Authorization, access-token headers and the forward-auth cookies are removed), since members can run code there (compiles). ESPHOME_TRUSTED_DOMAINS is the instance hostname (upstream's websocket Host/Origin check). Networking: bridge networks only, never host networking (the dashboard would then listen on every host address past the gateway, and instances would collide on port 6052), which is why several instances can run side by side. Without host networking there is no mDNS: the dashboard can't discover new devices or resolve .local, so give every device a fixed address it can reach (wifi use_address or manual_ip, or a DNS name your router serves). Online status then comes from the dashboard's ICMP ping sweep, and OTA updates and logs connect to that address from the container (outbound, routed through the host). Flashing over USB: the browser's Web Serial install (Chrome/Edge, HTTPS) works as-is; to flash from the server instead, set "Serial port" to the host device (e.g. /dev/serial/by-id/usb-...), passed into the container (only that one, not privileged; a path that doesn't exist on the host stops the container from starting). The Home Assistant ESPHome integration's dashboard link (firmware updates from Home Assistant) needs direct, unauthenticated access to the dashboard API and doesn't work behind the gateway; the devices' own native API (port 6053 on each device) is unaffected. Compiling downloads toolchains from the internet on first use (kept in the cache volume) and needs a few GB of memory and disk. The optional remote-build listener (Settings, off by default) is reachable only inside the instance's private network.

At every start the filmcraft-fetch init container downloads the release's filmcraft-web-.zip from GitHub, checks its SHA-256 against the pin before unpacking, and swaps the unpacked site into the filmcraft-site volume by rename; on any error it exits non-zero and the web server doesn't start (an unchanged pin skips the download). The host needs outbound HTTPS to github.com. The web server (nginx-unprivileged, read-only, no directory listing) answers only Traefik and itself. Version: the Release version / Release SHA-256 settings default to the pin in compose.yml (bumped with the template); set both together, from the release's SHA256SUMS.txt, to pin another release.

items.title: 🦊 Firefox Sync
items.text:
Self-hosted Firefox Sync server (bookmarks, passwords, history, tabs) for Mozilla accounts

Category: productivity Tags: firefox, sync, bookmarks, browser, mozilla Website: https://mozilla-services.github.io/syncstorage-rs/ Source: https://github.com/porelli/firefox-sync

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method custom SSO No Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_firefox-sync Subdomain firefox-sync

Auth Notes

Mozilla's syncstorage-rs 0.24.0 (Sync storage + tokenserver; upstream https://github.com/mozilla-services/syncstorage-rs), as built by porelli/firefox-sync (PostgreSQL image; links.source). Firefox signs in with a Mozilla account at accounts.firefox.com, then calls this server's tokenserver with that account's OAuth token, which the tokenserver verifies with Mozilla and exchanges for a short-lived storage token (1 h). Why no Portcullis sign-in (method custom, no native_login): Firefox makes every Sync and tokenserver request in the background as an anonymous request, without cookies, HTTP authentication or a client certificate (RESTRequest LOAD_ANONYMOUS, resource.sys.mjs fetch; tested by porelli/firefox-sync with a sign-in proxy and with mTLS: "no_node_found" / NS_ERROR_NET_UNCLEAN_SHUTDOWN). Portcullis sign-in, group-gate or a client-certificate tier in front of this host would break every Firefox, so the host is open (public@file, rate-limit; the tokenserver path /1.0/ the stricter rate-limit-auth; syncstorage-rs enforces its own request size limits) and access is decided by the server itself. Exposed on the host: GET /1.0/sync/1.5 (tokenserver: a Mozilla OAuth token with the Sync scope is required, 401 otherwise), /1.5//... (storage: Hawk-signed with this instance's secret, 401 otherwise), /heartbeat, /lbheartbeat, /version, /error (a test error), / and the API docs (/swagger-ui, /api-doc/openapi.json). No password, no sign-up page, no admin UI. Database roles: the internet-facing server connects as firefoxsync_app, which owns no table and is no superuser (it can't drop or disable the allowlist trigger, change session_replication_role or write the allowlist) and may create no database object (an event trigger; it keeps CREATE on the schema only for syncstorage-rs' no-op migration check). It runs no migrations; firefox-sync-migrate and firefox-sync-init use the owner and are not reachable. Who can sync: the Mozilla accounts on the allowlist, which is the uids the members of the access group (users_firefox-sync) entered themselves on My apps (Mozilla account ID; one uid per person, and no two people may register the same uid; admins may enter or clear one for someone), plus the instance's Other allowed accounts (uids not tied to a Portcullis person). The Hub writes them to the data file allowlist.json; at every start firefox-sync-init (guard.sql) installs exactly that list before the server starts, and a database trigger refuses every other account: no tokenserver row, no token, no storage. Nobody listed (the default) = nobody syncs; a missing, unparsable or invalid allowlist.json stops the instance (fail closed). Someone who leaves the access group drops off the list at the next delivery (the instance restarts within about a minute): that account's tokenserver rows are deleted, its tokens expire within the hour and it can't get new ones (its encrypted data stays, unreachable). Their entered uid is kept and comes back if they rejoin. Identity: Mozilla accounts, not Portcullis. Firefox has no way to use Keycloak or LLDAP for Sync (the self-hosted Mozilla accounts stack has no external OIDC login and is not published as an image), so the access group decides only who may register a uid, not who signs in to Firefox: whoever holds a listed Mozilla account can sync. Sync data is end-to-end encrypted with keys derived from the Mozilla account: this server, and whoever controls it, can't read it. Self-hosted Mozilla accounts (porelli/firefox-sync's fxa-mono option) are not offered: they need an SMTP server, MySQL and Redis, three more public hosts, a 5 GB image and 3-4 GB of RAM, and they are a second, password-based account system on the internet that Portcullis can't gate (Firefox calls the accounts API anonymously too). A separate template may add them later. The allowlist uses firefox-sync's table (sync_allowed_accounts) with a stricter trigger: it raises (no row, no token) instead of skipping the row, and an empty list refuses everybody instead of turning the allowlist off. Finding a uid: in a Firefox signed in to the account, Browser Console (devtools.chrome.enabled = true) - (await ChromeUtils.importESModule("resource://gre/modules/FxAccounts.sys.mjs").getFxAccountsSingleton().getSignedInUser()).uid - or let the person try: the refused uid is in the firefox-sync-db log ("portcullis: Firefox account is not on the allowlist"). Firefox setup: about:config identity.sync.tokenserver.uri = https:///1.0/sync/1.5 (Android: Sync Debug > Custom Sync server; iOS: Advanced Sync Settings), before signing in to the account. After a hostname change every Firefox must be pointed at the new URL; the accounts move to the new node at the next start. Node load: the tokenserver counts a new account in the node's load before the trigger refuses it, so one valid Mozilla token replayed would otherwise fill the node; every start sets the node's capacity to the maximum (2147483647) and recounts the load from its accounts. Residuals: the tokenserver needs outbound HTTPS to oauth.accounts.firefox.com. Upgrades: keep firefox-sync and firefox-sync-migrate on the same image; don't bump the PostgreSQL major.

items.title: 🍵 Gitea
items.text:
Lightweight self-hosted Git forge — repositories, issues, pull requests, packages

Category: devops Tags: git, forge, code-review, issues, packages Website: https://about.gitea.com/ Source: https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_gitea Admin Group admin_gitea Subdomain gitea

Auth Notes

Native OIDC through a Gitea OAuth2 authentication source ("Portcullis") that the gitea-auth job writes into Gitea's database at every start (client id, secret, discovery URL, groups), so a hostname, client or group change only needs a restart. Gitea loads the client id, secret and discovery URL when it starts, so a changed client secret takes effect once the gitea container itself restarts (rerunning the job is not enough); the required group and the admin group are read at every login. The client secret never appears on a command line: Gitea's CLI only takes it as an argument, so the job uses psql with the values read from its environment. The login page goes straight to Portcullis: there is no password sign-in form (POST /user/login answers 403), no sign-up form, no passkey or OpenID 2.0 sign-in, no HTTP basic authentication with a password and no reverse-proxy header auth. Nothing is readable without signing in (REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW). Any other authentication source added in the admin panel is switched off at the next start. Access: Gitea refuses the login ("Sign-in prohibited") unless the groups claim contains users_gitea, checked at every login. Admin: Gitea sets or clears the site-admin flag from admin_gitea at every login (an admin must also be in users_gitea). Everyone else is a regular user (the least-privileged full account; Gitea's "restricted" users can't see public repositories, so that role is left to admins). Removing a user from users_gitea blocks new logins only: open sessions, personal access tokens and SSH keys keep working (the AI tokens Portcullis minted are deleted); disable the user in Site Administration to cut access at once. Identity: accounts are created on the first Portcullis login, named after preferred_username (the immutable LLDAP username, not renameable in Gitea) and keyed on the OIDC sub. ACCOUNT_LINKING is disabled, so a login is never attached to an existing account by name or email (LLDAP emails are user-editable); a clash with an existing username or email is refused (an error page, no takeover). The email is only taken at account creation and kept private by default. Break-glass admin: Gitea makes the first account it creates a site admin and never demotes the last admin, so gitea-migrate creates the local admin portcullis-breakglass before anyone signs in (random password, never printed or stored) and gitea-auth keeps it admin with sign-in prohibited; Gitea won't start without it. To recover admin rights on the server, add a user to admin_gitea in LLDAP, or run docker compose -p portcullis- exec gitea-db psql -U gitea -d gitea -c "UPDATE \"user\" SET is_admin = true WHERE lower_name = ''". AI support (off until the admin turns it on): the official gitea-mcp server runs as the companion; every request runs as the person, with a Gitea access token named portcullis-ai- that the Hub mints on their first AI request (read-only mode: read scopes only, and gitea-mcp hides its write tools) and deletes when they leave the instance's population, when AI support or its mode changes and after a restore. A person who never signed in to Gitea gets no token. The hooks (portcullis/mcp-token.sh) list and delete tokens through Gitea's API as portcullis-hooks, a second local admin that gitea-migrate creates and gitea-auth keeps active: it has a discarded random password and no way in but an access token minted inside the container, one per hook run, deleted by that run. It never runs AI requests. Deleting it breaks AI support until the next start recreates it. AI and re-used usernames: the Hub sends the person's Keycloak id with every mint and the hook mints only for the Gitea account Gitea signs that id in to. If a person is deleted and their username given to someone new, the newcomer gets no token for the former person's account (the mint fails, shown on the AI tab; their web sign-in is refused as well): delete or rename the former person's Gitea account (Site Administration > User Accounts), then the newcomer signs in once. AI file writes: create_or_update_file can also delete files in the same commit (files[].delete) without a confirmation; the deletion is an ordinary commit, recoverable from the repository's history. While AI support is on, https:///mcp is the AI endpoint, so a Gitea user or organization named mcp loses its profile page (its repositories stay reachable): don't use that name. Git over HTTPS: clone https:////.git with your username and a personal access token (User Settings > Applications) as the password; git-credential-manager / git-credential-oauth can use Gitea's own OAuth2 provider instead. Git over SSH is off by default: turn on the "Git over SSH" setting and keep the SSH host port (default 2222, Gitea's built-in SSH server, keys from User Settings > SSH Keys); every instance needs its own host port. Webhooks and migrations to private addresses stay blocked (Gitea's defaults). Upgrades: the image is pinned; Gitea migrates its database on start and supports upgrading from older releases directly, but read the release notes of each major (28.x) before bumping. Keep gitea and gitea-migrate on the same image.

items.text:
Complete DevOps platform — Git, CI/CD, container registry, issue tracking

Category: devops Tags: git, ci-cd, devops, registry, issues Website: https://about.gitlab.com/ Source: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_gitlab Admin Group admin_gitlab Subdomain git

Auth Notes

Full OIDC with Keycloak. git-over-HTTPS, the API, the registry and CI runners are not behind forward-auth and work with personal access tokens. The sign-in, sign-up and OIDC paths (/users/...) are behind forward-auth + group-gate, so only members of users_gitlab can log in or have an account auto-created (GitLab CE has no OIDC group restriction; required_groups and admin_groups are Premium/Ultimate only). Existing GitLab sessions survive removal from the group until they expire; block the user in GitLab to cut access immediately. Admin rights are granted in GitLab (root account uses GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD); admin_gitlab is not mapped. Password logins outside the gated /users paths: GitLab's "password authentication for Git over HTTP(S)" and the OAuth password grant (/oauth/token, grant_type=password) are application settings, not gitlab.rb options, so the template can't switch them off. SSO-created accounts have no password (GitLab generates one nobody knows; resetting it goes through the gated /users/password); the root account's is GITLAB_ROOT_PASSWORD (generated). After the first start, turn off Admin > Settings > General > Sign-in restrictions > "Allow password authentication for Git over HTTP(S)" and enable two-factor authentication for root (GitLab refuses both for 2FA accounts). Identity: OIDC identities are keyed on preferred_username (uid_field, the immutable LLDAP username) and omniauth_auto_link_user is false, so an email match never attaches an OIDC login to an existing GitLab account (GitLab instead asks for that account's password). The email is not synced from Keycloak after the account is created. CA trust: GitLab's embedded OpenSSL uses the Hub's certs/ca-bundle.crt (system CAs + Portcullis' internal CA) in place of its bundled cacert.pem, so OIDC to auth. verifies with an ACME or internal certificate. Upgrades: the image is pinned; GitLab must be upgraded along its documented upgrade path (required stops between versions), never by jumping straight to the newest release.

items.text:

Category: monitoring Tags: monitoring, dashboards, metrics Website: https://grafana.com/oss/grafana/ Source: https://github.com/grafana/grafana

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method header-auth SSO Partial Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_grafana Admin Group admin_grafana Subdomain grafana

Auth Notes

Proxy auth with X-Forwarded-User header, accepted only from Traefik (GF_AUTH_PROXY_WHITELIST = PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP) and, while AI support is on, from the instance's grafana-mcp companion: its trust network mcp-trust (internal, members dashboards and grafana-mcp only) is added by trust.sh at every start, read from Grafana's own interface, without the gateway, broadcast and Grafana's own address. Auto-creates users. Each person's organization role (Viewer, Editor or Admin) comes from the instance's Role setting: group-gate sends it as X-Forwarded-Attr-Grafana-Role on every request and Grafana syncs it on every request (GF_AUTH_PROXY_SYNC_TTL 0). Members of the admin group are Admin by default, everyone else Viewer; other groups are set per group (privileged: only groups delegates can't steer). A role changed in the Grafana UI is overwritten by the next request. A request without the role header (the person's role can't be resolved, or group-gate can't read the Hub's attributes file) keeps the last synced role: Grafana doesn't fall back to Viewer, so remove a person from the instance's access group to take access away. Access gated by group-gate.

items.title: Public Exceptions
items.text:

items.title: 🧮 GridCraft
items.text:
Spreadsheet by ArtCraft, running entirely in the browser (Rust/WebAssembly; files stay on your device). In development.

Category: productivity Tags: artcraft, wasm, spreadsheet, office, data Website: https://getartcraft.com/apps/gridcraft Source: https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method forward-auth SSO No Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_gridcraft Admin Group admin_gridcraft Subdomain gridcraft

Auth Notes

In development upstream (https://getartcraft.com/apps): expect missing features and breaking changes between versions. GridCraft (https://github.com/storytold/gridcraft, Apache-2.0 OR MIT) is a static site: the app runs in the visitor's browser and has no user system, no server-side code and no server-side storage. Open uses the browser's file picker, Save/Export download files; preferences live in the browser's storage for this hostname. Portcullis sign-in (forward-auth + group-gate) is the only login; every member of the access group gets the same app (there are no roles). At every start the gridcraft-fetch init container downloads the release's gridcraft-web-.zip from GitHub, checks its SHA-256 against the pin before unpacking, and swaps the unpacked site into the gridcraft-site volume by rename; on any error it exits non-zero and the web server doesn't start (an unchanged pin skips the download). The host needs outbound HTTPS to github.com. The web server (nginx-unprivileged, read-only, no directory listing) answers only Traefik and itself. Version: the Release version / Release SHA-256 settings default to the pin in compose.yml (bumped with the template); set both together, from the release's SHA256SUMS.txt, to pin another release.

items.title: 🖥 Apache Guacamole
items.text:
Clientless remote desktop gateway — RDP, SSH, VNC in the browser

Category: remote-access Tags: rdp, ssh, vnc, remote-desktop, browser Website: https://guacamole.apache.org/ Source: https://github.com/apache/guacamole-client

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method header-auth SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_guacamole Admin Group admin_guacamole Subdomain remote

Auth Notes

Forward-auth + group-gate, then Guacamole's header extension trusts X-Forwarded-User, the immutable LLDAP username (never the user-editable email); accounts are auto-created with no permissions. The extension has no proxy allowlist, so a Tomcat RewriteValve rejects (403) any request carrying X-Forwarded-User that does not come from Traefik (PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP). On first boot the built-in guacadmin account gets a random password (GUACAMOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD) and a per-instance, non-guessable name, guacadmin- (both generated; break-glass only). The header extension logs a user in as the account named like X-Forwarded-User, so the same valve refuses (403) any X-Forwarded-User starting with "guacadmin" (case-insensitive): no LLDAP user can become the local administrator (also on databases initialized before the suffix, where the account is still called guacadmin). Set the Administrator setting before first enable to make that LLDAP user (by username, not email; not guacadmin*) the administrator instead. Accounts created when the header carried the email are named after it; rename them in the Guacamole UI. Connection permissions are managed in the Guacamole UI. Changing either value after the database is initialized has no effect. Upgrades: guacamole, guacamole-init and guacd are pinned to the same release and must move together; apply the upstream database schema upgrade scripts for each release in between before starting the new one.

items.title: 🌐 Headscale
items.text:
Self-hosted Tailscale control server with Headplane admin UI

Category: vpn Tags: vpn, wireguard, mesh, tailscale Website: https://headscale.net/ Source: https://github.com/juanfont/headscale

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_headscale Admin Group admin_headscale Subdomain vpn-admin, vpn

Auth Notes

Headscale uses OIDC for node registration. Users are keyed on the OIDC subject (iss + sub) and named after preferred_username (the immutable LLDAP username); email_verified_required stays true, so the user-editable, unverified LLDAP email is never synced. Write ACL policy users as "@", never by email. Headplane admin UI has its own OIDC client; it keys its users on sub and links them to the Headscale user with the same sub (its email fallback finds nothing because Headscale stores no unverified email). The first Headplane user becomes owner, later ones get the member role. No group-based access restriction — all OIDC users can register nodes. Post-start step for Headplane: create an API key with docker exec portcullis-<instance>-headscale-1 headscale apikeys create --expiration 365d (portcullis-headscale-headscale-1 for the default instance), paste it into the "Headscale API key" setting, then restart the app. Renew it before it expires. config.yaml is regenerated from the template on every start (so hostname and client changes apply), which means manual edits to it in the headscale-config volume are lost; change the template instead. Upgrades: Headscale is pinned; upgrade one minor release at a time (its database migrations do not support skipping) and pick the Headplane release that supports that Headscale version.

items.title: 🏠 Home Assistant
items.text:
Open-source home automation hub with dashboards, automations and integrations

Category: home-automation Tags: home-automation, smart-home, iot, dashboards, automations Website: https://www.home-assistant.io/ Source: https://github.com/home-assistant/core

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_homeassistant Admin Group admin_homeassistant Subdomain home

Auth Notes

Home Assistant 2026.10 has no OpenID Connect of its own; sign-in goes through the OpenID Connect custom integration auth_oidc (christiaangoossens/hass-oidc-auth, the integration HACS lists, here pinned to release 1.2.1 and installed by the homeassistant-init one-shot from the release asset after its SHA-256 matched; a mismatch stops the start. Its Python requirements ship in the Home Assistant image). It is the only auth provider: configuration.yaml (shipped read-only) sets auth_providers: [] so Home Assistant's own username/password login doesn't exist, and homeassistant-init marks onboarding done before the first start, so the onboarding wizard (which creates a password owner) never opens. The app is routed only while /auth/providers lists auth_oidc alone and onboarding is closed. Who can sign in: auth_oidc admits users in users_homeassistant (roles.user) and also users in admin_homeassistant alone (roles.admin implies access upstream), so the Hub's Keycloak access role (keycloak_access_role) restricts the client to users_homeassistant as well: in production only that group gets a token at all. admin_homeassistant members become Home Assistant administrators. Upstream sets roles only when the account is created (first login): change an existing user's administrator flag in Settings > People. Accounts are keyed on the OIDC issuer + sub, the display name is the LLDAP username (preferred_username), and SSO logins are never linked to existing accounts (automatic_user_linking off). No one is the instance owner; administrators can do everything an owner can except owner-only operations. Break-glass: there is no local login; an operator temporarily mounts a modified configuration.yaml (with a local provider) over the template's through the Hub's custom override. What works: the web UI and its websocket API (straight to Home Assistant, no forward-auth on the host), long-lived access tokens created by a signed-in user, and the Companion apps: upstream signs mobile apps in with a device code shown in the app and confirmed in a browser (Chrome/Safari or another computer) where the user signs in to Portcullis. That device-code step is phishable: a member can be tricked into entering a code an outsider's app shows, which signs that app in as the member (enter only codes from your own device). Limits: removing a user from the groups blocks new sign-ins only. Home Assistant refresh tokens stay valid until unused for 90 days and long-lived access tokens are effectively permanent (upstream has no session management or back-channel logout yet): deactivate the user in Home Assistant (Settings > People) to revoke them. Networking: the container is on Docker bridge networks only (never host networking, which would publish port 8123 past the gateway), so mDNS/SSDP/DHCP discovery, Bluetooth and USB radios are not available; use IP-based integrations (or MQTT / a network radio bridge). The HTTP server settings (Traefik as the only trusted proxy) are rewritten by homeassistant-init at every start; changes made in the UI don't persist. That is also why several instances can run side by side (instances: multi). Upgrades: read the Home Assistant and hass-oidc-auth release notes; bump auth_oidc (version and SHA-256 in init.py) together with Home Assistant when upstream requires it. AI support: the built-in MCP Server integration, with Home Assistant as its own OAuth server (people sign in through Portcullis); Home Assistant applies its own rules and Portcullis doesn't log or confirm its AI actions. Assist exposure is instance-wide, not a per-person boundary: every person's MCP client sees and controls the same exposed entities; the person's own account only decides attribution and whether administrator-only actions are allowed. Turning AI support on adds the integration with administrators-only off and the Assist API only; turning it off removes it, and the homeassistant service's entrypoint (portcullis/prestart.py) removes it again at every container start while AI support is off. A Home Assistant administrator can still add it by hand meanwhile: it then serves until the next container start (a restart from Home Assistant's own UI restarts only the process under s6 and doesn't run prestart.py). The AI hooks act as "Portcullis hooks", a system user prestart.py provisions with a new token at every container start: hidden from Settings > People, no credential of any sign-in provider (it can't sign in), local_only (Home Assistant then refuses its tokens from outside the local network, which still includes the LAN, not only this container). Its token lives in /config/.storage/auth, so instance backups carry it (rotated at the next start after a restore). When a person leaves while their account is matched, every Home Assistant refresh token of theirs ends (web sessions, Companion apps, long-lived tokens, AI clients); the account stays. The person is matched by the OIDC sub auth_oidc stored when they first signed in (the Hub sends each Keycloak id it saw for them), never by name: people can rename themselves. Someone the Hub couldn't match (no LLDAP uuid or Keycloak id recorded) costs everyone's AI client tokens of this instance when they leave, and their other tokens stay until an administrator deactivates or deletes them in Settings > People (the Hub lists them). An authorization code Home Assistant issued just before someone left stays usable for its 10 minutes. Switching AI support on or off ends every OAuth client token except Home Assistant's own web frontend and Companion apps; long-lived tokens are kept.

items.title: 📷 Immich
items.text:
Self-hosted photo and video backup with AI-powered search

Category: media Tags: photos, videos, backup, ai, gallery Website: https://immich.app/ Source: https://github.com/immich-app/immich

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_immich Admin Group admin_immich Subdomain photos

Auth Notes

Full OIDC with auto-register and auto-launch; password login is disabled while OIDC is configured. Storage quota and role come from the instance settings as the token claims immich_quota (GiB, -1 = unlimited) and immich_role: members of the admin group are Immich administrators (privileged setting), and Immich re-reads both at every sign-in. Trash days and machine learning are rendered into config.json at every start. Identity: OAuth users are keyed on the OIDC sub. Immich also links a login to an existing user with the same email and cannot be told not to, while LLDAP emails are user-editable; so on every start a one-shot job (immich-lock-local-users) gives local, unlinked users (such as the initial admin@portcullis.local) a placeholder OAuth id, and Immich then refuses the email link. Do not create local users in the Immich UI (they are only locked at the next restart); let users sign in with SSO instead. A user who unlinks OAuth in their settings is locked out of SSO until an admin clears the placeholder. Public exceptions (Hub, off by default): shared links still work for signed-in users; turning them on only matters when the policy requires a client certificate at the TLS handshake, which it then no longer does for any path of photos. (mTLS stays enforced at login via the Keycloak acr). Upgrades: immich-server and immich-machine-learning are pinned to the same release and must always move together; read the upstream release notes for breaking changes and keep immich-db on the image upstream specifies. Shared folders: immich-server runs as root (no compose user:), so External photo library declares runs_as uid 0 / gid 0, read-only; on a shared folder it joins the folder's group through group_add.

items.title: Public Exceptions
items.text:
Shared links (/share/<key>, /s/<slug>) for visitors without a client certificate. Immich's shared-link key, password and expiry still apply.

The app signs users in itself (native OIDC), so these paths are reachable without Portcullis sign-in anyway. When an admin turns them on in the Hub, they are also served without a client certificate on hosts whose policy requires one (see Public exceptions).

items.text:
Free and open-source media server — movies, TV, music, live TV

Category: media Tags: media, movies, tv, music, streaming, opensource Website: https://jellyfin.org/ Source: https://github.com/jellyfin/jellyfin

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Property Value Method native-oidc SSO Yes Group Access Group Admin Access Group users_jellyfin Admin Group admin_jellyfin Subdomain media

Auth Notes

SSO-Auth plugin with group enforcement. Users must be in access_group to log in. Members of admin_group get Jellyfin admin. The plugin is pinned (version + SHA-256, jellyfin/plugin.py) and installed by the jellyfin-plugin one-shot before Jellyfin starts (Jellyfin doesn't start if the download doesn't match); the plugin catalog is not used. The jellyfin-setup sidecar configures it at every start. Jellyfin's own login form stays on the ungated router (the Jellyfin apps use it), but no account set up by Portcullis can sign in with a password: SSO-created accounts get a random password and the plugin's authentication provider, and setup moves the local admin it creates to that provider too (setup then authenticates with its own API key, kept in the config volume). Break-glass: admin_jellyfin members are Jellyfin administrators through SSO. Local users an administrator creates by hand do get a password login there; avoid them, or use strong passwords. TV and mobile apps sign in with Quick Connect from a signed-in browser session. Identity: the plugin creates and matches Jellyfin users by preferred_username (the immutable LLDAP username; DefaultUsernameClaim) and never sees the email (no email scope). An SSO login whose username equals an existing local Jellyfin user (e.g. the LLDAP "admin" and the local admin created by setup) is linked to it. Shared folders: the jellyfin image runs as root (no USER, no compose user:), so the library settings declare runs_as uid 0 / gid 0, read-only; on a shared folder Jellyfin joins the folder's group through group_add.

Auth Notes

No public exceptions: Kanboard's router reads ?controller=&action= before the path (app/Core/Http/Router.php), so any public prefix would reach every APP_PUBLIC action, local password login included. Reverse proxy auth: users are matched on X-Forwarded-User, the immutable LLDAP username, honoured only from Traefik (TRUSTED_PROXY_NETWORKS = PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP). X-Forwarded-Email (user-editable) only fills the profile email and is ignored from other peers too. Auto-creates users on first login. The LLDAP user picked in "Kanboard administrator" (default admin = LLDAP's built-in admin) gets the Kanboard admin role; other roles are set in the Kanboard UI. Access gated by group-gate. Accounts created when the header carried the email are named after it; rename them to the LLDAP username in Kanboard.
