The tests cover the token rules (signature, issuer, audience, scope, client, LoA, population, Origin), resource metadata, protocol versions, tool policy, confirmations and continuations, rate limits, the access log (refusing unloggable calls), the aggregate (names, collisions, per-upstream rules) and the Portcullis proxy. The compose wiring check also asserts the gate's networks (exactly portcullis-mcp with the Hub and Keycloak, and portcullis-proxy at its fixed IP), its secret mounts, mcp_gate_data (read-only in the Hub) and that no router targets the Hub's port 8890.

items.title: build-and-test (whole stack)
items.text:
It boots the stack with a CI override (no ACME; self-signed server cert from the internal PKI) and verifies:

  • Vault
    • server-mode init and unseal, and the permissions on secrets/
    • after a restart it auto-unseals and the CA is unchanged
    • the enroll AppRole can only sign, list and read certs
  • PKI
    • the CA chain is created and valid
    • Vault issues client certificates
  • Keycloak
    • the OIDC discovery and SAML descriptor endpoints
    • the WebAuthn policy
    • the portcullis-forward-auth client
    • portcullis-forward-auth requires PKCE S256: an authorization request without a code challenge gets no code, the X.509 login with one does (oauth2-proxy's alpha.yaml must keep code_challenge_method: S256)
    • the invite post-broker flow admits only clients with the portcullis-invite-client scope (only portcullis-forward-auth, never a realm default), and a second keycloak configure keeps an extra-domain callback on portcullis-forward-auth while dropping a wildcard
    • LLDAP users show up through the federation
    • the email-unverified scope has exactly one mapper (email), also after a second keycloak configure; a throwaway direct-grant client with that scope instead of email gets email but no email_verified in the ID token, access token and userinfo, while the built-in email scope sends email_verified: false
  • mTLS
    • requests with no cert, or a cert from another CA, are rejected
    • cert info, including the serial, reaches the backend
    • requests arrive from Traefik's static IP
  • X.509 login
    • a login via Traefik with a real cert succeeds
    • the same cert as a forged header sent straight to Keycloak (from the portcullis and portcullis-auth networks and from 127.0.0.1:8080) must not yield an authorization code
  • Header spoofing. Client-supplied cert headers and their aliases are dropped, and group-gate's path rules see X-Forwarded-Uri.
  • Socket proxies. A real docker compose project runs through socket-proxy-hub, and the denied sections (build, swarm, plugins, secrets, system, ...) fail. Traefik's proxy is read-only.
  • Domains service (Pebble e2e). The image is built with GO_TAGS=testprovider (adds provider fake with records in memory + a DNS server on :8053). CI runs Pebble (-dnsserver domains:8053) and configures the service to use fake, Pebble's minica root, and DOMAINS_RESOLVERS=127.0.0.1:8053. It checks:
    • enrolling a domain, the records check, ACME DNS-01 order, serving the certificate
    • DELETE stops serving it
    • the served document contains only tls.certificates (no routers, services, middlewares)
    • every served certificate's SANs are exactly {<d>, *.<d>} for an enrolled domain
    • Traefik picks up the certificate by SNI within ~25 s without restarting (StartedAt unchanged)
    • core hosts still serve the main-domain certificate, never a certificate from the HTTP provider
    • Traefik's API lists no @http object (routers, services, middlewares, serverstransports)
    • mTLS refusal: the endpoint refuses requests without the client certificate
    • a kept domain survives backup/restore

The production image is built without testprovider (no fake provider).

  • Live Keycloak access role test (opt-in). When PORTCULLIS_KEYCLOAK_LIVE_URL (e.g. http://keycloak:8080) and PORTCULLIS_KEYCLOAK_LIVE_WIPE=portcullis are set, the Hub runs TestLiveClientAccess: it wipes realm portcullis, rebuilds it from the export, creates an LDAP group and a test client with the access role enforced, and drives the flow to verify the role is checked and fails closed. This is the live proof of contract §8. It requires a running Keycloak and is off by default.

  • Hub

    • runs as non-root
    • talks to Docker only via its proxy
    • answers 403 without the proxy secret
    • on a fresh install publishes the built-in default auth policy {factors: [mtls, webauthn], op: any} (either YubiKey method), which group-gate applies (step-up for a session with neither) to an app without its own policy
    • then gets a public default through PUT /api/settings, like an admin would; the revocation test checks that precondition, and every hand-written group-gate policy file in CI states its default explicitly
  • Enrollment UI and API. List users, sign a CSR with the AppRole token, list certs.
  • Passkey-only sign-in and setup links.
    • the browser flow has no password executor, has the identity-provider redirector, a passkey step and LoA 2 = allow-access; it carries the [sync <hash>] marker and a second keycloak configure rebuilds nothing
    • the LDAP federation has cachePolicy NO_CACHE (tests/test_shell_libs.sh also checks the realm export and that keycloak configure's patch sets it idempotently)
    • the invite identity provider is enabled, hidden, links existing users only (idp-detect-existing-broker-user, idp-auto-link), back-channel http://enroll:8445, PKCE; the service account portcullis-enroll has exactly view-users + manage-users
    • ./portcullis invite: link format, a new link revokes the older one, viewing doesn't consume it, a cross-site redeem is refused, portcullis-hub is refused, admin is allowed from the server
    • the Hub's invite API (enroll:8444, contract §9.4): 201 for a user, 409 for admin / portcullis-hub, 404 for an unknown user, 401 with a wrong secret; the Hub's copy of the secret matches; the JWKS serves an ES256 key
  • ./portcullis up and the Hub's LLDAP account. portcullis-hub is in lldap_admin, the 0640 / group 10001 password file logs in, a password changed in LLDAP is reset from the file on the next up, and the Hub sees /run/portcullis/lldap and /run/portcullis/invite.
  • Revocation end to end, once through ./portcullis cert revoke and once through Vault's CRL alone.
  • CLI. ./portcullis status.
  • Backup round-trip. It runs, in order:
    • ./portcullis backup with nothing stopped, then backup verify --local. A deliberately damaged backup must fail verification.
    • status --textfile.
    • backup --offsite twice to a local restic repository. The second run must be incremental, and retention must collapse same-day snapshots under keep-daily.
    • backup verify (off-host). A wrong BACKUP_PASSWORD must fail, and neither the root token nor the .env secrets may appear in the encrypted repository.
    • Restore into a fresh stack. Containers, volumes, .env, secrets/, certs/ and local backups are all deleted, as on a new host. Then restore --yes --from-offsite must bring back an active Vault, the Keycloak realm, the forward-auth client and the LLDAP user.

The step "Test the public guard (public exceptions) through Traefik" routes a test host through portcullis-public-guard@docker only and checks: no version-3 entry → 403; published prefix / static paths → 200; other paths, encoded / or #, dot-segment escapes → 403; Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, a credential header, credential cookies and query keys in PHP-mangled spellings → 403. The guard's unit tests are in tests/test_group_gate.py (PublicGuardTest, PhpVarNameTest).

items.title: e2e (browser)
items.text:
tests/e2e/e2e_login.py runs Playwright Chromium (pinned in tests/e2e/requirements.txt) with a CDP virtual WebAuthn authenticator against the full chain: Traefik → oauth2-proxy → Keycloak (LLDAP users, WebAuthn, X.509) → group-gate. A whoami test app has three hosts: app. (group users_e2e, /admin → admin_e2e), hwk. (WebAuthn policy) and mtls. (mTLS policy).

Scenarios:

No user has a password and nothing is pre-assigned in Keycloak: the job creates one-time setup links with ./portcullis invite <user> --to <landing> --json (for e2e, e2e-other, e2e-bypass and the bootstrap admin) and the test starts from them. Any password field fails the test.

  1. An unauthenticated request is redirected to a passkey-only Keycloak sign-in page.
  2. The setup link → Register my key → passkey registration → the webauthn-policy app (hwk.), with no second prompt.
  3. The setup link works once.
  4. The session reaches the app.
  5. Apps get the username as X-Forwarded-User, and spoofed identity headers are dropped.
  6. path_groups: /admin needs admin_e2e. /%61dmin, //admin, /x/../admin and /ADMIN are denied, while /administrator is allowed.
  7. A second login in a fresh browser with the same key is one passkey assertion.
  8. Group denial for a user not in users_e2e (also onboarded by setup link).
  9. The bootstrap admin's link lands on the portal (https://<domain>/) with the Hub link.
  10. An unused setup link, redeemed and then steered to another client's authorize endpoint with kc_idp_hint=portcullis-invite (client e2e-invite-bypass, created by the job), is denied by the invite post-broker flow: no code for the client, no passkey registered.
  11. X.509 login via Keycloak satisfies an mTLS policy.
  12. An mTLS session without the cert on the request is refused (mTLS binding).
  13. A revoked client cert is rejected.
  14. A client cert from a foreign CA is rejected in the TLS handshake.

tests/e2e/e2e_invite.py <setup-link> <landing-url> runs the setup-link checks (registration, no password, acr/amr = hwk, single use, one-touch second login, the invite identity provider refuses browsers without a link) against any running install, e.g. a live server with a throwaway user (E2E_IGNORE_HTTPS_ERRORS=1 for ACME staging). With --reinvite-cmd "<command printing portcullis invite <same user> --json>" it also registers a second, new authenticator through a second link and checks that both keys sign in — or, with --replaced (--replace-keys), that the old one no longer does. The e2e job runs both variants after the browser tests (users e2e-spare, e2e-lost). Dialogs are answered like a user pressing OK (the default value).

After the browser tests, the job enables the monitoring profile and checks:

  • all monitoring services become healthy, and every Prometheus target is up
  • the Vault health probe and the enroll/forward-auth/LLDAP probes succeed
  • group-gate, CRL, backup (textfile), CA-expiry, Traefik and Vault metrics are present
  • the alert rules are loaded, and neither VaultSealedOrDown nor CrlStale is pending or firing
  • Grafana at metrics.<domain> redirects unauthenticated users to sign in, and rejects a forged identity header that doesn't come from Traefik's IP

On failure, screenshots, HTML, traces and service logs are uploaded as artifacts. The test needs a live stack and is not collected by pytest.

items.title: e2e-instances (app instances, extra domains)
items.text:
The whole stack plus the Hub, the domains service against Pebble with the fake DNS provider, and the enrolled domain team-b.test (enrolled on the domains API with the fake provider, which the Hub refuses; the Hub picks it up from the service's list). The Hub's only template source is the CI template tests/e2e/apps/echo (traefik/whoami behind Portcullis sign-in, plus a hold service that ignores SIGTERM so a backup can be made slow), seeded into hub_data as a local source. Through the Hub's API the job creates echo-a and echo-c on team-b.test and echo-b on the main domain (echo-c with policy mtls), checks the published policy file (v5, host keys, groups per instance, extra_domains), the rendered labels (portcullis-auth-ext and the /oauth2/ router to forward-auth-ext on extra-domain hosts only), the callbacks on portcullis-forward-auth and the SNI certificate. Then tests/e2e/e2e_instances.py:

  • cross-domain SSO: signed in on the main domain, echo-a opens with no further WebAuthn assertion, through the host's own callback, PKCE S256 and a host-only __Host-portcullis_ext cookie; a stale ext cookie signs in again without a loop; echo-c steps up to mtls exactly once (a returning user's passkey session, the client certificate available);
  • two instances, two groups: each user reaches only their instance;
  • a backup longer than 60 s through hub.<domain>: 202, a concurrent request 409, the op record ends ok (Traefik keeps its default timeouts).

Finally, on the real daemon: backup (the helper image pulled by digest, helpers removed), the typed-id delete (refusals first, then containers, volume and routing gone, the backup listed), restore into a new id (file and volume-root owners and modes kept, the new volume labelled for its project, the instance enables).

items.title: e2e-settings (app settings panel)
items.text:
The whole stack plus the Hub (built from the same-named Hub branch, like e2e-instances) with one local template source: the templates repo's immich, grafana, nextcloud and firefox-sync (from the same-named templates branch, else main) and two CI fixtures, tests/e2e/apps/settings-echo (traefik/whoami with a per-person option delivered as the header X-Forwarded-Attr-Tier) and settings-file (per-person options in a data file people.json, restart on membership changes, and a hook that stores every input it gets). A Traefik alias override puts auth.<domain> and the app hosts on portcullis-proxy, so Immich and Nextcloud reach Keycloak as they would through public DNS. Users are created in LLDAP; groups, memberships, enables and settings go through the Hub's API, the way an admin makes them. Then tests/e2e/e2e_settings.py runs 19 checks in a real browser with virtual passkeys:

  • Sign-in: alice, bob and carol follow their setup links, register a passkey and reach the portal.
  • Claims (Immich): alice (in office_milan, row 10 GiB) has quotaSizeInBytes 10 GiB in /api/users/me and in Immich's UI; bob (in admin_immich, the template's preset row) is an Immich admin with the 100 GiB default.
  • Headers: bob is a Grafana org Admin on his first and later requests, alice a Viewer; settings-echo receives alice's gold and bob's bronze tier, and never another host's header.
  • Data file: people.json inside the settings-file container lists only the people with access.
  • Person-entered values (Firefox Sync): alice enters her Mozilla account uid on people.<domain> (200); bob's identical uid is refused with 409 and the answer doesn't name alice; carol, outside the access group, gets
  • After the debounce, allowlist.json in firefox-sync-init lists only alice's uid, the init ran once, and on the real Postgres her uid gets a tokenserver row while an unlisted one is refused.
  • Membership changes: one batch through the Hub (alice leaves office_milan and joins admin_immich, bob leaves admin_grafana, three people join users_settings-file). Both removals end the person's Keycloak session (the Hub signs removed members out), so alice and bob must sign in again, and any other sign-in prompt fails the test. Then: alice's next Immich sign-in has the 100 GiB default and admin rights (a role changed on an existing account), her tier is bronze, bob is a Grafana Viewer, people.json lists four people, settings-file restarted exactly once for the three joins (counted from a live docker events stream), and the hook got the full state with trigger membership_change.
  • My apps: carol's /api/me/apps lists only settings-file with her values and no other username; /api/instances/immich/settings on people.<domain> is 404.
  • Leave and rejoin: alice leaves users_firefox-sync: the file no longer lists her, her tokenserver rows are deleted and nobody can sync (an empty allowlist lets nobody in); she rejoins and syncs again.
  • Custom fields with _: a field cost_center (LLDAP attribute cost-center) set on alice shows in the overview, fills a rule group cost_center = "CC-42", reaches settings-echo as X-Forwarded-Attr-Cost-Center and Keycloak's example access token for Immich's client as attr_cost_center.
  • Hooks (Nextcloud): the first install applied the default quota through the start hook (occ config:app:get files default_quota is 10 GB).

Timing bounds come from the Hub: a membership delivery arrives within one 60 s debounce window plus the evaluator's minute and slack. Secrets reach the test only through the environment or curl -H @<(…), never on argv. Failure artifacts hold the settings panels (secrets are write-only), the policy and attributes files, the data files (never *.secrets.json), container logs, screenshots and traces. The traces start after the setup-link sign-in; the setup pages' screenshots still show the (consumed) setup links, and traces carry session cookies of the throwaway stack.

items.title: e2e-folders (shared folders and the doctor)
items.text:
Built like e2e-settings (the same-named templates and Hub branches, else main; the Traefik alias override; the Hub's data seeded with one local source): the templates repo's jellyfin (the step fails if it has no folder block) and the CI fixture tests/e2e/apps/folder-writer (alpine as user: "2001:2001" with umask 022, a read-only root filesystem and no capabilities; its option shared has folder: {access: write, runs_as: {uid: 2001, gid: 2001}}; it writes a new file into /shared at every start and has a lan_only TCP port WRITER_PORT, default 18765). Before the stack starts, the job installs acl, checks that /srv is ext4 and takes ACLs, and builds /srv/e2e-media: 6 directories 0750 and 50 files 0640, all 1000:1000.

tests/e2e/e2e_folders.py (Python standard library only, no browser) drives the Hub's admin API, sudo find / getfacl and docker through 14 scenarios, every count exact:

Scenario Checks tree 50 files and 6 directories as built, no ACLs enable jellyfin and folder-writer enable; the writer can't write yet and created no file check Check path's summary is exactly exists · ext4 · ACLs and xattrs supported · 50 files · owners 1000:1000 (all) create folder media gets gid 60000, not adopted preview the preview's lines (gid allocated, "50 files and 6 folders change group 1000 → 60000", group 1000 keeps its access through an ACL on 56 entries, both apps stopped for under a minute); nothing changed on disk apply the operation succeeds: 56 entries, a snapshot, 2 uses added host verify every entry has gid 60000 and its old owner; directories 2770 with group:1000:r-x in the access ACL and a default ACL of group::rwx, mask::rwx, other::--- and no entry for group 1000; files 0660 with group:1000:r-- writer file the writer's new file is 2001:60000, mode 660 despite umask 022 jellyfin its process has gid 60000, lists the library, and can't write (read-only file system) no drift a disk check newer than the request finds no folder_owner finding drift after a chgrp 1000 of the writer's file, exactly one folder_owner Warning offering reapply_folder and undo_folder undo the preview says 56 entries go back, 0 changed since; after the undo every original entry has its exact original owner, group and mode and no ACL, and the folder has nothing left to undo exposure WRITER_PORT on 0.0.0.0 is one lan_only_exposed Warning; Rebind… to 127.0.0.1 leaves docker port showing only 127.0.0.1:18765, and the finding is gone proxy the Hub's socket proxy is unchanged from main, the Hub has no Docker socket, and no fixer helper container is left

A scenario that builds on a failed one fails too. On failure the job uploads e2e-folders-artifacts: logs, API answers, the tree and getfacl -R, the Hub's folder data, snapshots and the doctor cache.

items.title: e2e-filesharing (file-share passwords, SMB3 hardening, revocation)
items.text:
tests/e2e/e2e_filesharing.py (Playwright, smbclient 4.19.5) provisions a stack with Samba and Time Machine instances, tests per-person credential creation (fresh passkey touch, the password shown once), SMB3 connections with encryption required, revocation latencies (hub-made removal, LLDAP-direct removal, writer demoted to reader), instance and core restores voiding credentials, that no hash appears in any backup or log, and the F58 capability ruling (smbd signals work without CAP_KILL). Scenarios:

  • Setup: connect_address, ports on 127.0.0.1, size_limit 500GiB / office_milan 10GiB, folder slot via assignment, readers / writers before enable, testparm hardening.
  • Sign-in via setup links (alice, bob, carol); fresh auth popup flow (COOP, the authorize parameters, the password once, replay refused).
  • SMB3 sessions: Time Machine and Samba list shares, carol writes as 21002:60000, encryption required, SMB2/NTLMv1/guest/wrong password refused, outside-LAN client refused.
  • Revocation: hub-made ≤ 10 s, LLDAP-direct ≤ 75 s, writer demoted ≤ 4 s (session gone, login refused). Measured at 0.8–0.9 s, 3.4–51.8 s, and about 3.6 s.
  • Restore: instance restore → credential voided, card says "reset by a restore", re-create works. Core restore → no hash in 45 backup files, hub_secrets emptied, credentials voided, uid pool +1000, Samba restarted from Hub.
  • No hash visible: docker inspect, container logs, hub_data, audit, ops, archives, state.yaml.

Built like e2e-settings (same-named Hub and templates branches, else main). Ubuntu 24.04 runners, smbclient pinned at 2:4.19.5+dfsg-4ubuntu9*. On failure: policy/attributes files, data files, container logs, screenshots, no traces (DOM snapshots would carry the password).

items.title: e2e-ai (AI support through mcp-gate)
items.text:
The first run of the whole chain: an MCP client on the runner host → Traefik → mcp-gate → the Gitea companion (the official gitea-mcp, from the templates repo) → Gitea, with Keycloak's OAuth (PKCE and resource, the Hub's portcullis-ai-claude-code client and its mcp:* scopes) and the Hub (AI settings, the companion switch, the gate files, lazy mint and revoke hooks). The Hub's template source is the same-named templates branch (else main) with gitea, grafana and the CI echo fixture; the CI fixtures declare ai.unsupported. Setup goes through the Hub's admin API as the CI admin root: instances gitea-b and a throwaway echo-del, gitea, gitea-b and grafana enabled, alice / bob / carol in their groups, the master switch on with Claude Code offered (admin flag on), Gitea's companion in read_write, Grafana's (identity headers) read-only.

tests/e2e/mcpclient is a stand-in for Claude Code on the official MCP Go SDK (pinned in its go.mod):

  • mcpclient login --client-id <id> --callback-port 33418 --resource <url> [--scope "<scopes>"] --token-file <f> [--ca-file <pem>] [--timeout 5m] prints the authorize URL (Playwright opens it, signs in with a CDP virtual authenticator and consents), serves the loopback callback and writes the token to the file (0600; tokens are never printed or put on argv);
  • mcpclient call --url <url> --token-file <f> --method tools/list|tools/call [--tool <name> --args <json>] [--protocol <version>] [--elicitation url [--elicit-answer accept|decline|cancel]] [--ca-file <pem>] prints one JSON document (the result, the negotiated protocol and any elicitation/create requests, or the HTTP status and WWW-Authenticate). --elicitation url declares URL-mode elicitation only and turns off the SDK's automatic retry, so a 2026-07-28 input_required is printed as sent.

tests/e2e/e2e_ai.py scenarios:

  1. gitea_as_alice: a token for https://gitea.<d>/mcp, tools/list, and a repository listing that shows only alice's repositories.
  2. leaver_refused_and_revoked: alice removed from users_gitea → 403, and her portcullis-ai-* Gitea token deleted.
  3. audience_separation: her Gitea token at gitea-b, mcp.<d>, hub.<d> and people.<d> → 401; one token for two resources (both audiences asserted; Keycloak not minting it fails the scenario) → refused at both.
  4. no_token_crossing: the MCP token on Gitea's and the people pages → a sign-in redirect or 401, never a page; browser cookies on /mcp → 401. This proves the apps refuse the MCP token; that the gate never forwards it rests on mcp-gate's unit tests.
  5. destructive_confirmation: root's delete_instance on hub.<d>/mcp → the confirmation link; bob can't open it; root types the id and touches a fresh passkey → approved; the retry runs, a second one needs a new confirmation; audited via: ai with the client and the confirmation id.
  6. aggregate_lists: on mcp.<d> carol sees gitea__*, grafana__* and portcullis__my_apps and calls Grafana through the gate (identity headers); bob sees no grafana__*; root sees no admin tool.
  7. ai_off: the master switch off → every resource 503. While the apps restart, a companion host answers 404 (its router is gone with the app), which fails closed too.
  8. companion_confirmation: alice's label_write delete_repo_label → a people.<d> confirmation (typed check: the instance label); bob 404; approved → runs once with the canonical arguments; changed arguments → a new one; the access log's confirmation_id.
  9. url_elicitation_2026: with URL elicitation declared, a 2026-07-28 call gets input_required (a Hub D tool and a companion tool); a 2025-11-25 session gets the gate's elicitation/create (mode url) and the Hub's text.
  10. gitea_isolation: the gitea-internal and companion alias resolution, no portcullis-hook-* token left after mint and revoke, the switch-on's revoke_all succeeded.
  11. companion_alias_guard: ./portcullis status shows no name takeover for the real Gitea and Grafana companions; a container outside the instance's project answering to portcullis-mcp-gitea--gitea is flagged, and the real one with it as sharing the name.

Not covered: an approved 2026-07-28 round trip through requestState, the gate's continuation of a confirmed call the companion then asks input for, and token refresh. Built like e2e-settings (same-named Hub and templates branches, else main). Tokens live only in a temp directory outside the artifacts. On failure: logs, screenshots and traces.

e2e-instances runs on ubuntu-latest: the echo fixture's hold service has its own pinned busybox image, so the Hub's helper image isn't in use when the job removes it (Docker's containerd image store refuses to remove an image in use).

Cross-repo branches. ci.yml also runs on workflow_dispatch. On a branch whose name exists in porelli/portcullis-hub (not main, not a tag), .github/actions/hub-image builds the Hub from that branch instead of pulling edge; the Hub's build.yml likewise tests against the same-named branch of the templates and core repos, else main.

items.title: Caching
items.text:
Core CI caches what it safely can. Caches are written only on pushes to main.

  • Infra and monitoring images: cached by the local composite action .github/actions/cached-images.
    • The cache key is a hash of each job's pinned image list. Refs without a digest are refused.
    • After docker load, every name set by the tarball is removed. Each ref is then re-pulled by its pinned digest (with retry and backoff), so the engine reuses a loaded image only if its content-addressed ID matches the registry's config digest.
  • enroll and group-gate images: buildx layer cache (type=gha).
  • Go: module and build cache through setup-go, with go mod verify.
  • Python: pip and Playwright browsers, cached on the pinned requirements file (group-gate/requirements.txt has --require-hashes).

The revocation check waits up to 180s, because Vault rebuilds delta CRLs at most once a minute.

items.title: Releases (release.yml)
items.text:
Runs on v* tags:

  1. preflight checks two things:
    • The tag is vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and CHANGELOG.md has its ## [X.Y.Z] section.
    • The HUB_IMAGE default in docker-compose.yml is ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:A.B.C@sha256:…, where vA.B.C is a published (non-draft, non-prerelease) Hub release and the tag still resolves to that digest.
  2. ci runs the full ci.yml on the tagged commit.
  3. release builds a reproducible portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz (the checkout without .git, plus VERSION) and its .sha256. It then creates the GitHub release with the changelog section, the pinned Hub image and generated notes.

See Upgrading & Releases.

items.title: Dependabot
items.text:
.github/dependabot.yml proposes weekly, grouped updates for:

  • the compose images
  • the enroll Dockerfile and Go modules
  • the GitHub Actions
  • the e2e Python requirements

Image constants in the CLI and inline images in workflows are not covered by Dependabot. They are still checked by the pin-enforcement step.

items.title: Auto-merge
items.text:
Core, the Hub and the templates share one auto-merge workflow, .github/workflows/dependabot-automerge.yml. Its logic lives in .github/automerge/automerge.sh, which is identical in all three repos and tested by .github/automerge/test.sh. The workflow runs after the required workflows finish on a Dependabot PR and never checks out PR code:

  • Patch, minor and digest-only updates are squash-merged once every required workflow passed on the PR's head commit. The PR must be Dependabot's own single, GitHub-signed commit.
  • Majors (or updates of unknown type) get the major-update label and stay open.
  • Pre-releases are closed.
  • Red CI opens an update-failed issue.

A merge that fails although CI passed gets at most one re-attempt. Only GitHub's "Base branch was modified" error is re-attempted. It happens when another PR merged at the same moment. The workflow waits about 10 seconds, then tries the merge once more at the same tested commit. Anything else, such as an HTTP 5xx, is not retried. If the merge still fails, the run fails and its error names the cause and the command to retry by hand:

gh workflow run dependabot-automerge.yml -f pr=<n> -f dry_run=false

Run it from a checkout of the repo, or add -R porelli/<repo>. Check the PR first: a 5xx can still have merged it. Leave out -f dry_run=false to see the decision without acting on it.

The workflow doesn't ask Dependabot to rebase. Dependabot ignores @dependabot rebase comments posted with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN (or by any GitHub App) and replies "only users with push access can use that command".

items.title: Running the core tests locally
items.text:
python3 tests/test_group_gate.py
bash tests/test_cli.sh
bash tests/test_shell_libs.sh
(cd enroll && go test ./...)
shellcheck -S warning portcullis scripts/lib/*.sh tests/*.sh
# compose validity without Docker containers:
PORTCULLIS_ROOT=/tmp/x ./portcullis init --env-only --non-interactive --domain ci.example.org --dns-provider none

items.title: lint.yml: every push and PR, forks included
items.text:
No secrets, no core checkout, read-only token. Safe for fork pull requests, so every contributor gets this feedback:

  • python tests/validate.py: the manifest schema plus repo rules (networks, volumes, middlewares, required vars, mounts, image pinning, header trust, Dependabot coverage, .core-ref). See Manifest Reference → Validation.
  • bash tests/compose-config.sh: docker compose config for every template.
  • shellcheck of the test scripts and template scripts.
  • actionlint (pinned image).
  • python -m unittest discover -s tests: the validator's own tests, including AITests (the ai: block rule for rule with the Hub's ValidateAI: both forms, companions, identity modes, reserved names and variables, trust networks, the ai.chat rules).
  • tests/trust/test_grafana_trust.sh: Grafana's trust.sh (the AI trust network allowlist) against stubbed ip output, including the ambiguous layouts it must refuse.

items.title: test-apps.yml: integration tests
items.text:
Triggers: push to main, pull requests to main (from forks too: core is public and no job uses a secret), and manual workflow_dispatch (inputs pr, ref, apps; apps = all tests every template). Dependabot's image bumps are pull requests, so each runs the tests of the app it touches. It boots core infrastructure and, for the affected templates, runs tests/apps/<app>.sh and then the sign-in e2e. The trust boundary is per job:

Job Secrets What it does gate none Resolves what to test. Fork PRs run like any other PR (core is public; no job uses a secret), with .core-ref taken from the PR's base. For a manual run with pr = <n>, it resolves the PR head commit to test changes none Verifies the commit under test. Picks the apps: changed <app>/ directories and changed tests/apps/<app>.sh. A change to tests/lib.sh, tests/app-images.sh, tests/e2e/, .github/ or .core-ref tests all apps. With no usable base, all apps are tested fetch-core none Checks out nothing from the PR except .core-ref, read from a trusted commit (for PR runs: the PR's base, so a PR can't point CI at another core ref). Clones the public core repo anonymously at that ref, resolves the infra image list with docker compose config --images against a throwaway .env from portcullis init --env-only (failing on an empty list), packs core as an artifact, and writes the infra image cache app-images (matrix per app, push to main only) none Never runs for PRs or manual runs. For each tested app whose test boots it, reads the image list from its compose.yml (tests/app-images.sh), pulls the pinned images and writes that app's image cache (key: hash of the list). Starts no container e2e-browser (push to main only) none Installs the hash-pinned tests/e2e/requirements.txt and that Playwright version's Chromium and writes their cache (key: hash of the requirements). Runs no template code test (matrix per app) none Downloads core by artifact ID with digest verification. Writes no cache. Loads the cached infra and app images as untrusted: removes every name a tarball sets, then binds each image (core's and the app's) with a docker pull of its tag@sha256 pin. The pull checks the manifest against the pinned digest and reuses a loaded image only if its ID (the hash of its config, which pins every layer) is the one that manifest names; otherwise it downloads the image fresh. Boots infra like core's own CI: every secret generated by portcullis init --env-only (the workflow sets none, since the shell environment would override .env), Keycloak with its production start command, setup through the core CLI (vault init, pki setup --with-server-cert, config apply --bundle-only, keycloak configure, oidc register). Checks Traefik got its static IP and that forward-auth redirects an unauthenticated request to auth.<domain>, then runs the app's shell test and its sign-in e2e. Uploads e2e-<app> (screenshots, page HTML, traces, logs) on failure

Every job has a read-only contents: read token. The workflow deliberately does not use pull_request_target, which would run fork code with a write token.

Fork PRs get the full integration tests automatically. A maintainer can re-run one with Actions → Test Apps → Run workflow, pr = <number>. That run tests exactly the PR's head commit, and aborts if the head moved.

.core-ref holds the core ref the templates are tested against: a tag such as v1.4.0, or main during development (today: main). Changing it re-tests every template.

items.title: Per-app sign-in e2e
items.text:
tests/e2e/app_signin.py (Playwright with a CDP virtual WebAuthn authenticator, like core's e2e job) proves a real person can sign in to each app through Portcullis and gets the right role. Driven by the manifest's tests.signin, per app:

  1. LLDAP users without passwords: e2eadmin (access + admin group), e2emember (access group), e2eoutsider (no group);
  2. what the Hub would do: the template's Keycloak clients (secret = the app's generated env, which the workflow creates once for the shell test and the e2e), the group-gate policy file (access_group per host, auth.admin_paths; its version is read from core's group-gate);
  3. the app started with tests/lib.sh compose_up, containers ready;
  4. per user, portcullis invite <user> --to https://<host><path> --json opened in Chromium: passkey registration, then the app's own sign-in (its SSO button, the OIDC / SAML round trip, or forward-auth);
  5. results: member signed in with its username and not admin, admin has admin rights, outsider refused (group-gate's 403 or the app's denial); any password field fails unless the manifest documents it; an outsider refusal when nobody could sign in is reported inconclusive.

expected_fail marks known failures: reported, not fatal, only when the failure matches the entry's match (and not its not_match) in that check's own evidence: its detail, the pages its flow saw, the app's logs since its flow started. A flow the test broke (password field, Keycloak/enroll or browser error, never on the app) or an exception fails, and a marked check that passes fails the run so the marker is removed. Where group-gate decides (forward-auth, header-auth, and the login-path gates of GitLab, LiteLLM and Vaultwarden) only group-gate's own refusal counts for the outsider: its HTTP 403, its "not authorized" page and its DENIED user=… host=… log line. Each setup link must register exactly one passkey. Today: the outsider check of the native-OIDC apps with no group restriction of their own that let every test user in (Headscale/Headplane, Immich): with the Hub, its Keycloak access role (keycloak_access_role) refuses outsiders at Keycloak, but CI has no Hub (the test registers plain clients), so the role is not applied there; the member check of the apps that admit only their first user (the owner) and users the owner adds or approves (Actual Budget, NetBird); the member and admin checks of Nextcloud, whose HTTP client refuses a local TLD (.local) or private address for Keycloak (match: "violates local access rules"; its outsider check is then inconclusive) — the test never widens an app's access to make a check pass. skip: docs (public), Plex (custom, plex.tv). Each run starts the app from fresh volumes.

CI stand-ins for public DNS: every app hostname is a network alias of Traefik on portcullis-proxy (apps reach auth.<domain> for OIDC discovery and the token exchange) and is in the runner's /etc/hosts (the browser). Chromium trusts core's root CA through an NSS database. Results go to the job summary; on failure the e2e-<app> artifact holds every step's screenshot and HTML, a Playwright trace per user (playwright show-trace), the app's container logs and core's logs.

items.title: docs-dispatch.yml
items.text: On push to main it sends a templates-updated repository_dispatch to this docs repo, which regenerates the App Catalog. It needs the DOCS_DISPATCH_TOKEN secret. Without it the step is skipped with a notice, and the docs pick the change up on their daily rebuild.

items.title: craft-releases.yml
items.text:
Weekly (and on dispatch), tests/craft-releases.sh bumps each Craft template's pinned web release (${CRAFT_VERSION:-…} / ${CRAFT_SHA256:-…}) to the latest release of storytold/<app>, once the GitHub asset digest, SHA256SUMS.txt and the download agree, and opens one PR per app on craft/<app>-<ver>. It uses only GITHUB_TOKEN (contents, pull-requests, actions: write). PRs opened with that token start no pull_request workflows, so the script dispatches Test Apps (pr=<n>, apps=<app>, core ref from the PR's base) and Lint (on the branch) for each PR it opens; workflow_dispatch is the one event GITHUB_TOKEN may start. The Test Apps run is dispatched on the base branch, so its check attaches to the base commit, not the PR: the script links the run in the PR body.

AI support in the app tests. gitea.sh, grafana.sh, nextcloud.sh and homeassistant.sh run their mint / revoke / on_change hooks the way the Hub does (argv verbatim, JSON on stdin, split output) and check that a credential never reaches an argv or a log. nextcloud.sh starts the companion and checks per-person identity (one person's app password sees only their files; no credential, nothing; a bad one, 401). grafana.sh checks the trust network (internal, exactly Grafana and the companion, Grafana's allowlist without the gateway, broadcast and its own address) and that a spoofed X-Forwarded-User from elsewhere on portcullis-proxy isn't signed in. ai-chat.sh renders librechat.yaml from ai-providers.json (secrets only as ${VAR} references, a refused file fails closed), checks the access-group restriction and the MCP OAuth callback. write_ai_providers_override (below) emulates the Hub's delivery to an AI page.

items.title: Test helpers (tests/lib.sh)
items.text:
Area Functions Output pass, fail, info, section, report Waiting wait_for_url URL TIMEOUT NAME, wait_for_container Keycloak keycloak_admin_token, keycloak_user_token, keycloak_enable_direct_grant, keycloak_register_client LLDAP lldap_token, lldap_graphql, lldap_create_user, lldap_create_group, lldap_add_to_group, lldap_sync_keycloak Compose compose_up APP, compose_down APP, app_container_ip APP, app_logs APP Assertions assert_http_code URL CODE, assert_redirect_to_keycloak URL, assert_redirect_contains URL STRING, assert_body_contains URL STRING, assert_container_can_reach CONTAINER URL Public exceptions public_routed_prefixes <manifest> <all\|listed> [token…] prints what the Hub's public router opens; write_public_override <app> <service> <host-arg> <tier> <out> <entry…> writes the override labels the Hub would generate (tier for every router, public router behind portcullis-public-guard@docker with static-only supporting paths, exact paths, strip middleware); pass it to compose_up with COMPOSE_OVERRIDE=<file>. write_public_policy <sub> <manifest> <mode> writes the version-3 policy entry the Hub would publish into core's hub_data volume, so core's real public guard runs (clear_public_policy empties it). assert_public_path <host> <path> [curl args] / assert_gated_path … / assert_public_refused … send HTTPS requests through Traefik on the runner (no client certificate) and check the app answers / the request is redirected to auth.<domain> / the guard answers 403. grafana.sh uses them: a listed dashboard token is public; an unlisted token, /, /api/user and /public/build/ stay gated; Grafana login cookies (also PHP-mangled spellings), Authorization, X-Access-Token and auth_token query variants are refused by the guard. It needs a core with /public-guard (.core-ref). nextcloud.sh and immich.sh check their path lists statically Settings data files write_appfiles_override <app> <name> <json> <out> writes <name>.json the way the Hub does (a directory per file, mode 0640 group 10001 where the runner can set it) and an override that bind-mounts that directory read-only at the files[] entry's mount; pass it with COMPOSE_OVERRIDE=<file>. write_appfile <app> <name> <json> rewrites the file atomically (restart the service after). firefox-sync.sh uses them to check that only the file's uids can sync and that a bad or missing file stops the instance. The public-exception override also strips the template's header deliveries, as the Hub's public router does Header trust assert_traefik_only_trust <compose> <SETTING> checks statically that the trust setting uses ${PORTCULLIS_TRAEFIK_IP:-…} and nothing trusts every peer. assert_spoofed_identity_rejected <url> [expected] sends a forged X-Forwarded-User from the CI host (never Traefik) and expects a rejection. Required for header-auth templates

compose_up mirrors the Hub: before each compose call it exports a random value for every manifest env: entry with generate: random that isn't set yet. Templates reference those as ${VAR:?}, so a missing value fails loudly.

Every template needs a tests/apps/<app-id>.sh (validate.py checks it). A static test is the minimum; copy tests/apps/scrutiny.sh. What the tests typically verify:

Auth method Checks forward-auth Unauthenticated request redirects to Keycloak; container healthy; app endpoints respond header-auth The above, plus the Traefik-only trust setting and a rejected spoofed identity native-oidc Container reaches Keycloak's discovery endpoint; the app's SSO redirect points at Keycloak; gated login/admin paths redirect public / custom App responds without authentication; container healthy

See Adding an App for a template.

items.title: Hub CI (build.yml)
items.text:
Triggers: pushes to main, tags v*, and pull requests. Every action is pinned by commit SHA.

  • test:

    • gofmt -l . must be empty
    • go vet ./...
    • go test -race -count=1 ./... (after installing acl, so the ACL codec is checked against the kernel's setfacl bytes)
    • folderfix root tests: sudo go test -tags fixerroot ./internal/folderfix/ runs the shared-folder fixer as root on real files: ACLs, setgid, must_own, hard links, setid files, file capabilities, other mounts, devices, unreadable entries, apply, snapshot, restore and its dry run. Under CI these tests fail instead of skipping when root, ACLs, getfacl or mount are missing.
    • fixer helper docker tests: go test -tags docker -run TestDocker ./internal/hub/ with a required Docker daemon builds a Hub-shaped image and runs the real fixer helper: scan, snapshot, apply, verify and restore on a real volume; its capabilities, no-new-privileges, uid, network, read-only root filesystem and process limit from inside; every capability dropped in turn (each mode needs exactly its set); and the Hub finding its own container ID from its mountinfo.
    • go build ./cmd/hub

    The unit tests cover validation, strict route parsing, the policy-file writer (collisions, deny group, snapshots, expiring array, user-attributes.json), middleware (proxy secret, CSRF), per-app locking, reconcile/drift, the Engine API client, the LLDAP client (GraphQL + LDAP Password Modify), the Keycloak client (attribute mappers), the rule parser, and the directory service (users, groups, fields, rule evaluator, exceptions, expiries, CSV import, delegated permissions, protected accounts parity). New packages: internal/rules (rule parser and evaluator), internal/directory (users, groups, fields, permissions, import, audit). TestRealTemplates loads a sibling portcullis-templates checkout if present. TestPeopleListenerHasNoAppRoutes checks that the people listener registers exactly the directory routes plus the nine caller-only My apps routes (GET /api/me/apps, PUT and DELETE /api/me/apps/{instance}/values/{key}, POST and DELETE /api/me/apps/{instance}/credentials/{key}, GET /api/me/ai, DELETE /api/me/ai/connections/{client}, GET /confirm/{id}, POST /api/me/confirmations/{id}), and no app/policy/drift/compose/settings/Docker routes. AI support is tested per package: internal/aigate decodes and re-encodes the shared §15.4 vector byte for byte (the same files as mcp-gate's internal/config/testdata/); the gate files (populations, clients, fail-closed rebuilds), the credential store (TestHubHoldsNoAgeIdentity: no Hub code can decrypt), mint and revoke (single flight, exit 3, leavers, app_oauth records), the switches, the confirmations, the Keycloak AI clients against the kctest realm, and the Portcullis MCP: every tool's twin both ways (TestAdminToolsSameAsHTTP, TestPeopleToolParity), no secret argument name (TestNoSecretArgNames), no token echoed by any tool (TestTokenNotEchoed), the per-call classes. TestLiveAIObjects runs the AI client checks against a real Keycloak when PORTCULLIS_KEYCLOAK_LIVE_URL and PORTCULLIS_KEYCLOAK_LIVE_WIPE=portcullis are set (not in CI; it wipes realm portcullis). Docs copies. The Hub ships some pages of this site as MCP resources (portcullis://docs/<name>), committed under web/docs/ (web/docs/sync.sh: integration-contracts.md, hub.md, auth-policies.md, groups.md, backups.md, file-sharing.md). After changing one of them here, run PORTCULLIS_DOCS_DIR=<docs checkout> go generate ./web in the Hub and commit; TestDocsCopiesInSync fails on drift when PORTCULLIS_DOCS_DIR is set (CI doesn't set it). A new page goes into both sync.sh and docsPages in web/web_test.go. The harness also serves AI fixtures (the Hub listener has its own fake fresh-auth verifier at /harness/authorize, signing in as root, for the admin confirmation page): an app with token and identity-header companions, an app_oauth app, a fake connections store and access log, and the people MCP switched off for one user (no card). The settings code is tested per package: the template settings validator, the setting types (parsing, rendering, resolution), the delivery engine (data files, claims, headers, hooks, reload, debounce, stale runs), person-entered values (uniqueness, population, purges, the refused-save limit) and the settings API (admins only, secrets never returned). A build-tagged harness (go test -tags harness -run TestHarness -timeout 0 ./internal/httpapi) serves the UI on 127.0.0.1:18888 (and the people page on :18889) against in-memory fakes, for checking the panels in a browser. TestProtectedAccountsParity reflects over directory.Service methods to check every user-targeting operation refuses admin and portcullis-hub. - build (after test): - Multi-arch image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) with SBOM and provenance (mode=max) attestations. - Tags X.Y.Z/X.Y/X/sha-<short> for release tags and edge for main. latest is disabled. - Pushed to GHCR and signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub OIDC) by digest. Pull requests build but don't push or sign.

Verify a published image with the command in Hub → Image tags.

items.title: AI support manual checklist
items.text:
The checks CI can't make: real Claude clients, a hardware passkey and a live Keycloak. Use throwaway users and instances on the test server and clean them up afterwards.

  1. Deploy. Merge in order docs → core → Hub → templates; deploy to the test server (./portcullis upgrade); confirm mcp-gate healthy and ./portcullis status clean.
  2. Live checks:
    1. Settings → AI on; Gitea AI support on (read_write); the People card for a test user shows the URLs.
    2. Claude Code on the operator's machine: the card's claude mcp add command, /mcp sign-in with the passkey; list the test user's issues; create one (write) and ask to delete a repo → confirmation page with passkey; remove the user from users_gitea → refused.
    3. claude.ai custom connector with "Use your own OAuth client" (portcullis-ai-claude, no secret): connects (spec call 40; if it demands a secret, apply call 40's fallback and note it).
    4. hub.<d>/mcp as an admin: get_instance, doctor_findings, delete a throwaway instance through the confirmation.
    5. An ai-chat instance with an OpenAI-compatible provider: a chat that lists the person's Gitea repos through the aggregate.
    6. The access log and audit.jsonl show the calls with via: ai; no secret in either (grep the markers used).
  3. Report what passed, the builder verifications' results, anything deferred.

Also check, from the builders' reports:

  • Claude desktop custom connector with "Use your own OAuth client" (public client, PKCE); Claude Code claude mcp add + /mcp; the card's steps as written, for the aggregate and one app.
  • The AI page with an OpenAI-compatible Ollama and the Anthropic API, and with a LiteLLM instance:
    1. getent hosts auth.<d> mcp.<d> inside <instance>-api-1 shows Traefik's IP;
    2. a member connects "All my apps": consent on the instance's ai-chat-mcp client, the callback, tools listed, a tool call as that person; the access log's client is the instance's ai_client;
    3. a second instance (ai-research): its own client ai-research-ai-chat-mcp and its own callback host;
    4. the refresh lifetime without offline_access: decide whether to add it;
    5. an outsider is refused by Keycloak's access role on the real Hub, not only by LibreChat (the ai_client keeps the instance's access role and flow: EnsureClientAccess on an AI client hasn't run against a real Keycloak yet);
    6. a provider change restarts the instance and the selector shows the new labels; a cleared key drops that endpoint.
  • Passkey sign-in on an AI client gives acr / amr hwk (TestLiveAIObjects skips it: it needs a WebAuthn authenticator).
  • Fresh-auth popup on both hosts: a confirmation approved on people.<d> and one on hub.<d> (the https://hub.<d>/ redirect URI), with the passkey's auth_time and amr verified by the real Keycloak.
  • Home Assistant (app_oauth): in claude.ai add a custom connector for https://<host>/api/mcp; Claude discovers the protected-resource and authorization-server metadata and uses its CIMD client id; the redirect goes Home Assistant /auth/authorize → auth_oidc → Keycloak (passkey) → "continue on this device" → Claude's callback; Assist tools appear (GetLiveContext); a non-admin member turns an exposed light on. The same with Claude Code (loopback, port 33418). Removing the person from the group ends the connection after the next reconcile (at most 10 minutes for a pending code). The host must be publicly reachable and not need mTLS.
  • Nextcloud: AI on; alice uses claude.ai through https://<nextcloud host>/mcp; leaving revokes the app password (up to 10 s of lag); a restore runs revoke_all.

items.title: Running workflows locally with act
items.text:
act runs GitHub Actions workflows locally in Docker:

act -l -W .github/workflows/test-apps.yml                     # list jobs (templates repo)
act -j lint -W .github/workflows/lint.yml                      # static checks, no secrets
act -W .github/workflows/test-apps.yml                         # integration (no secrets needed)
act -W .github/workflows/ci.yml                                # core CI (core repo)

The first run downloads the runner images, which can take a few minutes.

items.title: Upgrading & Releases
items.text:
Upgrade an installation from the core checkout with:

git pull
./portcullis upgrade

upgrade is safe to re-run. Every step it performs is idempotent, and it backs up first.

items.title: What portcullis upgrade does
items.text:
1. Fills in missing secrets. It generates HUB_PROXY_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET, FORWARD_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET, LLDAP_JWT_SECRET or BACKUP_PASSWORD if they are empty or missing. Nothing on disk depends on those. The database and admin passwords must already be in .env, and the command stops if one is missing.
  2. Checks the networks. It validates the portcullis-proxy and portcullis-auth settings in .env against the existing Docker networks, and stops with instructions if they differ.
  3. Backs up with portcullis backup, a consistent online backup: Vault raft snapshot, pg_dump, the LLDAP/Hub/ACME volumes, .env, certs/ and secrets/. It goes to backups/<timestamp>/. Skip this with --skip-backup.
  4. Pulls images. Core images are pinned by digest in docker-compose.yml, so the pull only changes something when the pins changed in the commit you pulled. The Hub image comes from HUB_IMAGE (see below).
  5. Re-runs the setup steps.
    • vault init: unseal, enroll AppRole and policy.
    • pki setup: rewrites the client-cert role, so a changed CLIENT_CERT_TTL applies to new certificates, and refreshes the Keycloak truststore and CRL settings. An existing CA is never replaced.
    • Rebuilds certs/ca-bundle.crt.
  6. Restarts the stack with docker compose up -d --build and waits for Vault, PostgreSQL, LLDAP and Keycloak to be healthy. Traefik, forward-auth and Keycloak are restarted if the CA chain or truststore changed.
  7. Re-applies the identity config. It runs keycloak configure (realm settings, X.509/CRL settings, scopes, LDAP bind) and oidc register (client secrets from .env), then recreates forward-auth so it picks up a newly generated client secret.
  8. Refreshes the Hub's templates. It has the Hub sync its template sources (SIGHUP; the Hub also syncs at every start, so a recreated Hub has already done it) and prints each source's result: up to date, updated to <commit>, or not updated and why. A newer Hub rejects template versions it no longer accepts and denies their apps (fail closed); this step makes sure it judges the current templates, not the checkout of the previous run. A failed pull keeps the previous checkout, and a version that would take an enabled app's template away is reset to the previous one — nothing is opened. Apps still without a valid template are named, with the fix. An older Hub image (one that doesn't report syncs) gets a warning instead: press Sync All Sources in the Hub's Template Sources tab. See Template sources.

It also checks the Hub image: before the upgrade it warns when HUB_IMAGE is pinned (in .env or the environment: a pinned Hub doesn't move with core), and after the start it compares the Hub's policy file version with the one group-gate serves (and looks for group-gate's "is not supported" log line). On a mismatch it prints the fix — drop or align HUB_IMAGE, then ./portcullis up — and never fails the run: until then group-gate denies every app request (the Hub and core must be upgraded together).

Check the result with ./portcullis status.

Apps enabled in the Hub are separate compose projects. upgrade does not restart them. The Hub reconciles them on start and reports anything that is not running as drift.

items.title: Backups and rollback
items.text:
The backup made by upgrade is a normal local backup (see Backups). It contains the Vault unseal key and root token, so it can decrypt the CA. Protect it like the keys themselves. upgrade does not upload it off-host: run ./portcullis backup --offsite first if you want an off-host copy of the pre-upgrade state.

To roll back, check out the previous core commit (or release) and restore the backup:

./portcullis restore --list
./portcullis restore backups/<timestamp>

restore saves the current .env, secrets/ and certs/ to backups/pre-restore-<timestamp>/ before overwriting them.

items.title: Versions and releases
items.text:
How the four repositories are versioned is defined in Integration Contracts §1:

  • Tags. Every repo uses semver tags vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. A breaking change to an integration contract bumps MAJOR in every repo it affects.
  • Core images are pinned tag@sha256:digest in every compose file and profile, so a core commit fully determines which Traefik, Keycloak, Vault, LLDAP, oauth2-proxy, PostgreSQL, socket-proxy and monitoring versions run. Dependabot proposes updates weekly; CI fails on anything unpinned.
  • Templates. The Hub tracks the default branch of each template source; it pulls updates at every start, during ./portcullis upgrade and with Sync All Sources in the Hub. The templates CI tests against the core ref in its .core-ref.

Check what you run:

./portcullis version          # core version (VERSION file or git describe) + Hub image
./portcullis version --json

items.title: Core releases
items.text:
A core release is a vX.Y.Z tag. .github/workflows/release.yml publishes it only if all of the following holds:

  1. Tag and changelog. The tag is vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and CHANGELOG.md (Keep a Changelog) has a ## [X.Y.Z] section.
  2. Pinned Hub. The HUB_IMAGE default in docker-compose.yml is a released Hub tag pinned by digest (ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:A.B.C@sha256:…). That tag must be a published, non-prerelease Hub release that still resolves to that digest.
  3. CI. The full core CI (ci.yml, called as a reusable workflow) passes on the tagged commit.

Then it publishes:

  • release notes: the changelog section, the pinned Hub image, and GitHub's generated notes
  • portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz: the checkout without .git, plus a VERSION file. The tarball is reproducible: sorted, numeric owner, commit time
  • portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz.sha256

Install or upgrade from a release tarball:

sha256sum -c portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf portcullis-X.Y.Z.tar.gz && cd portcullis-X.Y.Z

Or check out the tag in your git checkout: git fetch --tags && git checkout vX.Y.Z.

items.title: Hub image
items.text:
HUB_IMAGE selects the Hub:

  • On core main the default is ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:edge, the latest build of the Hub's main.
  • A core release pins a released Hub tag by digest, as described above.

  • Overriding it in .env? Use a released tag and its digest, never edge in production:

    HUB_IMAGE=ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3@sha256:<digest>

Hub releases are published as X.Y.Z, X.Y, X and sha-<short>. There is no latest tag. Each image is signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub OIDC). Verify it before you pin it:

cosign verify ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/porelli/portcullis-hub/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/porelli/portcullis-hub:1.2.3   # top-level Digest:

No releases yet

No repository has been tagged yet. Core main therefore runs the Hub's edge, and the templates CI tests against core main. CHANGELOG.md collects everything under [Unreleased].

items.title: Upgrade notes
items.text: Changes that need an admin action when you upgrade. The templates repo keeps the same notes in its CHANGELOG.md.

items.title: App instances and extra domains (Hub v5, core v5, templates contract v2)
items.text:
• Nextcloud admins must be in users_nextcloud. The Nextcloud template now sets keycloak_access_role: Keycloak lets only members of the instance's access group (users_nextcloud for the default instance, users_<instance-id> for others) sign in. A member of admin_nextcloud who isn't also in users_nextcloud could sign in before (user_oidc's group whitelist) and is now denied. Before you upgrade, add every Nextcloud admin to users_nextcloud (Hub → Users & Groups).
  • Paperless-ngx, Vaultwarden and GitLab set keycloak_access_role too; their sign-in already required the access group, so nothing changes for their users.
  • Vaultwarden runs with SSO_ONLY: the email + master password login is off; the master password only decrypts the vault after the SSO login.
  • Jellyfin: the local admin account loses its password login (setup moves it to the SSO plugin's provider). Administrators sign in through SSO (admin_jellyfin).
  • Guacamole: header logins as guacadmin* are refused (403). Databases created from now on name the built-in administrator guacadmin-<generated suffix>.
  • The Hub and core must be upgraded together (policy file version 5, see above).
  • Missing app groups. Enabling an app now creates its missing users_<id> / admin_<id> groups as the enabling admin. Apps enabled earlier whose groups don't exist (e.g. users_headscale, users_vaultwarden, users_actual-budget deleted in LLDAP) let nobody sign in: the App Catalog shows them in a Missing groups banner — click Create missing groups, then add the people who need access (Missing groups).
  • Keycloak forgets users and groups deleted in LLDAP. keycloak configure (run by upgrade) sets the LDAP federation to remove its copy of a user LLDAP no longer has (at the user's next lookup — the Hub lists all users every 15 minutes; Keycloak's LDAP sync itself never removes users) and to drop Keycloak groups LLDAP no longer has at the next sync (hourly). Copies left by earlier deletions go within about 15 minutes (users) or an hour (groups) after the upgrade. Nothing is removed while LLDAP is unreachable. Core's own accounts are not affected: the federation is read-only (Keycloak never writes LLDAP), local Keycloak users and the master realm's admin are never checked against LDAP, and the Hub's service account portcullis-hub is filtered out of the federation on purpose. Never start the stack with an empty or wrong LLDAP database (a lost lldap_data volume): Keycloak would then remove every user's copy, passkeys included, at their next sign-in attempt. Restore LLDAP from a backup first (Backups: restore refuses to start Keycloak over an empty LLDAP). The Hub's cleanup pauses itself when LLDAP looks wrong (Stale Keycloak records).
  • Failed hostname changes are not re-applied. The Hub now keeps the last hostname change in its own record. A hostname change that failed under an older Hub isn't re-applied after the upgrade: repeat it once (save the same hostnames again).

items.title: Changing settings during an upgrade
items.text: You changed Run ACME_STAGING or MTLS_ENABLED ./portcullis config apply && ./portcullis up CLIENT_CERT_TTL ./portcullis upgrade (or ./portcullis pki setup); only new certificates are affected FORWARD_AUTH_CLIENT_SECRET ./portcullis oidc register && ./portcullis up An empty rotatable secret (to rotate it) ./portcullis upgrade generates a new one HUB_IMAGE ./portcullis up Network ranges See Security & Hardening → Networks. Docker can't change an existing network in place

items.title: TLS Certificates & mTLS
items.text:
Portcullis has two TLS toggles in .env. They are independent of each other:

Setting .env variable Default What it controls Certificate source ACME_STAGING false Staging (test) vs production (trusted) Let's Encrypt certs Client certificates MTLS_ENABLED true Whether Traefik requests mTLS client certs (PIV/YubiKey)

After changing either one, run:

./portcullis config apply
./portcullis up

config apply rewrites traefik/dynamic/tls.yml (Traefik hot-reloads it), sets ACME_CA_SERVER in .env, and rebuilds certs/ca-bundle.crt. up recreates Traefik when its environment changed.

items.title: Production (ACME_STAGING=false, the default)
items.text:
• Uses the Let's Encrypt production CA, which all browsers trust.
  • Rate limits apply: 50 certificates per registered domain per week.
  • One wildcard certificate (<domain> + *.<domain>) covers every app, so individual subdomains never appear in Certificate Transparency logs.

items.title: Staging (ACME_STAGING=true)
items.text:
• Uses the Let's Encrypt staging CA. There are no rate limits, but browsers will not trust the certificate. Use it while you iterate on DNS setup.
  • App containers that call Keycloak over HTTPS mount certs/ca-bundle.crt. config apply builds it from the system CAs, the internal Portcullis PKI chain, and the Let's Encrypt staging root (only when ACME_STAGING=true). init, up and upgrade rebuild it too.

Browser workarounds for staging certs: start Chrome with --ignore-certificate-errors, accept the risk in Firefox, or use curl -k.

items.title: Switching
items.text:
1. Set ACME_STAGING=true or false in .env.
  2. Run ./portcullis config apply && ./portcullis up. config apply notices the flip and clears Traefik's acme.json, so Traefik requests a new certificate.
  3. Wait about 2 minutes for the DNS-01 challenge: docker compose logs -f traefik 2>&1 | grep -i acme.

items.title: TLS tiers
items.text:
With MTLS_ENABLED=true, Traefik offers three TLS option sets (traefik/dynamic/tls.yml):

Tier Traefik option Behavior protected RequireAndVerifyClientCert Client cert required. Without one, the TLS handshake fails authaware VerifyClientCertIfGiven Client cert optional. Verified against certs/ca-chain.crt if present public NoClientCert No client cert requested

All core routers (auth, hub, enroll, traefik, directory) use authaware. For apps, the Hub derives the tier from the app's access policy and writes it into a per-app compose override. You change it by editing the policy in the Hub, not the template's compose.yml.

items.title: Issuing certificates
items.text:
Client certificates come from Vault's PKI (pki_int, role client-cert). The key is generated on the YubiKey and never leaves it.

  • Admin enrollment: at https://enroll.<domain> (requires lldap_admin), either by pasting a CSR made with ykman or through the guided flow, or on the host with ./portcullis cert enroll <user> [email].
  • What Vault signs: the role takes the CN from the caller, never from the CSR, and enroll only signs CSRs whose subject is exactly the user. The certificate has the clientAuth EKU.

items.title: Lifetime and renewal
items.text:
Certificates live CLIENT_CERT_TTL, default 720h (30 days).

Why 30 days. A very short lifetime (say 24 hours) would mean renewing with the YubiKey every day; in practice certificates expire and users fall back to weaker factors. A short lifetime would only be standing in for revocation, and Portcullis enforces revocation everywhere a certificate is accepted (see Revocation), so the lifetime just sets how often people renew. 90 days (2160h) is reasonable if you revoke lost keys promptly.

./portcullis pki setup (also run by upgrade) rewrites the Vault role with the current value. Only certificates issued afterwards are affected.

Self-service renewal at https://enroll.<domain>/self is open to any signed-in user, for their own certificate only. It runs on router enroll-self with portcullis-self@docker, which is group-gate's /authenticated check: revocation and host checks, but no lldap_admin requirement. Renewal succeeds only if all of these hold:

  • the browser presents the user's current, valid, unrevoked certificate (Traefik passes it to enroll via client-cert-pem@file)
  • its CN is the signed-in user
  • Vault issued exactly that certificate
  • the pasted CSR is for the same public key: ykman piv keys export 9a + ykman piv certificates request

An expired or revoked certificate cannot be renewed this way. An admin re-enrolls the key instead.

CLI renewal on the host, with the YubiKey attached: ./portcullis cert renew <user>.

Expiry warnings. These list users whose newest certificate has fewer than CERT_EXPIRY_WARN_DAYS (default 7) days left:

  • ./portcullis status (and vault.certs_expiring in status --json)
  • ./portcullis cert list, which marks them expiring
  • the enrollment UI, which flags them

items.title: mTLS login through Keycloak
items.text:
auth.<domain> uses the authaware tier, so the browser can present the YubiKey cert to Keycloak:

  1. Traefik verifies the cert against certs/ca-chain.crt.
  2. Traefik forwards it PEM-encoded in X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert (middleware client-cert-pem@file).
  3. Keycloak reads the header with its built-in traefik x509 lookup provider (--spi-x509cert-lookup--provider=traefik). The provider understands Traefik's passTLSClientCert pem: true format.

The realm's X.509 authenticator (x509-config) then:

  • maps the Subject CN to the LLDAP username
  • re-validates the chain against certs/truststore/ (written by pki setup, mounted as Keycloak's truststore), and checks the validity period and the clientAuth EKU
  • checks the CRLs at http://vault:8200/v1/pki_int/crl and .../crl/delta (##-separated in crl-relative-path). Keycloak caches each for at most 60 s. pki_int has auto_rebuild=true (keeps the full CRL from going stale) and therefore enable_delta=true: Vault does not rebuild the full CRL on revoke. New revocations land in the delta CRL, rebuilt every minute, until the next full rebuild. ./portcullis cert revoke also rotates the full CRL immediately
  • fails closed on the CRL: if the CRL cannot be fetched, the X.509 login fails. x509-cert-auth-crl-abort-if-non-updated=true (Keycloak's actual key, with a dash) also rejects a CRL past its nextUpdate. Vault never lets it get that stale: pki setup sets pki_int/config/crl to expiry=72h auto_rebuild=true auto_rebuild_grace_period=12h

./portcullis keycloak configure pushes the x509-config settings from keycloak/realm-export.json to an existing realm.

items.title: Trusted proxy address
items.text:
A cert header carries only the public certificate, so anyone who could put one in front of Keycloak could log in as that user. Three things prevent it:

  • Keycloak only trusts the header from Traefik. Keycloak's header-based lookup providers (traefik included) return no certificate unless the request comes from a trusted proxy (HttpRequest.isProxyTrusted()). With --proxy-trusted-addresses=${PORTCULLIS_AUTH_TRAEFIK_IP}, Keycloak (Quarkus) decides that from the TCP peer address of each request, and overwrites any X-Forwarded-Trusted-Proxy header the client sent (ForwardedParser, run before routing). The only trusted address is Traefik's fixed IP on the internal portcullis-auth network. That IP is outside the network's dynamic range, so no other container can get it. These sources are untrusted, so the cert header and their X-Forwarded-* are ignored:
    • requests via 127.0.0.1:8080 (the CLI's admin API access; it arrives from the Docker gateway)
    • requests from the portcullis network
    • requests from any other container attached to portcullis-auth
  • Traefik strips client-supplied cert headers. It deletes X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert* sent by the client on the entrypoint, also for requests without a TLS client cert, and drops their _/. aliases (aliasHeadersStrategy=delete).
  • CI tests it. The build-and-test job logs in through Traefik with a real cert, which must succeed. Then it sends the same cert as a forged header straight to Keycloak from the portcullis and portcullis-auth networks and from 127.0.0.1:8080, with the realm's HTTPS requirement temporarily off so only the proxy gate can stop it. None may yield an authorization code.

See Security & Hardening.

items.title: Sign-in levels (Keycloak browser flow)
items.text:
The realm's browser flow portcullis-universal (kept equal to keycloak/realm-export.json by ./portcullis keycloak configure) has no password:

acr (LoA) Satisfied by amr pwd (1) the client cert (automatic when the browser presents one) or a passkey mtls / hwk hwk (2) reaching LoA 1: every LoA 1 factor is hardware-backed, so no second touch (same) mtls (3) the client cert mtls

oauth2-proxy asks for hwk by default; group-gate asks for mtls when a policy needs the cert. Keycloak's step-up on an existing session asks only for the levels it has not reached (no prompt=login).

A user's first passkey comes from a one-time setup link (./portcullis invite <user>, or the Hub): Keycloak 26.8 cannot enrol a passkey from inside the flow (WebAuthnPasswordlessAuthenticatorFactory.isUserSetupAllowed() is false). The setup link signs the user in through the hidden identity provider portcullis-invite (enroll) with LoA 2 / amr hwk, after the passkey registration it requires. Details: Security & Hardening and Authentication Policies.

items.title: mTLS binding (group-gate)
items.text:
A token with amr=mtls proves that a cert was used at login. Sometimes an app's policy is satisfied only through the mtls factor:

  • mtls alone
  • all including mtls
  • any where mtls is the only factor present in the token

Then group-gate also requires the current request to carry a client cert that is not revoked and whose CN equals the session's preferred_username. Otherwise the user gets the step-up page (acr_values=mtls).

So a session opened with a cert that is revoked later stops working immediately. So does a session replayed from another browser without the key.

items.title: Revocation
items.text:
./portcullis cert list                # find the serial (--all includes revoked)
./portcullis cert revoke <serial>     # revoke (add --yes to skip the prompt)
./portcullis cert sync                # rewrite the serial list from Vault

Traefik does not check CRLs. A TLS handshake with a revoked but unexpired cert still succeeds. Revocation is enforced in three places:

  1. group-gate, on every request (portcullis-groups@docker and portcullis-self@docker). client-headers@file (Traefik passTLSClientCert with serialNumber: true) passes X-Forwarded-Tls-Client-Cert-Info to the backend and to every later forward-auth middleware. group-gate returns 403 when the cert's serial is revoked, before any other check. It has two sources:
    • The serial list certs/revocation/revoked-serials.txt. cert revoke and cert sync rewrite it atomically from Vault's list of revoked serials, and group-gate re-reads it when it changes. If Vault can't be queried, the file is left unchanged and the command fails: it never "un-revokes" by writing an empty list. If the file exists but can't be read, group-gate denies every request that presents a cert (fail closed).
    • Vault's full and delta CRL (GATE_CRL_URL = http://vault:8200/v1/pki_int/crl, GATE_DELTA_CRL_URL = .../crl/delta), re-fetched every 60 s (GATE_CRL_REFRESH_SECONDS). The union is enforced. It also covers revocations made directly through the Vault API or UI: they reach the delta CRL within about 2 minutes (Vault's periodic rebuild runs once a minute) and are denied at group-gate's next refresh. If Vault is unreachable, the last good copy of each CRL is kept and the serial list still applies.
  2. Keycloak X.509 login: the CRL check above. It fails closed when the CRL is unavailable or stale.
  3. mTLS binding: sessions on mTLS-only policies need the unrevoked cert on every request.

Coverage. Revocation covers:

  • every router whose middleware chain has client-headers@file before portcullis-groups@docker (all core routers and the default templates)
  • new Keycloak X.509 logins
  • sessions on mTLS-only policies

Not covered. Routers that rely on the TLS client cert alone, e.g. a protected-tier router without portcullis-groups@docker. There the cert works until it expires. Password and WebAuthn sessions of the same user are also not affected; sign them out in the Keycloak admin console if needed.

items.title: Vault: server mode, auto-unseal and AppRole
items.text:
Vault runs in server mode with integrated (raft) storage on the vault_data volume (vault/vault.hcl, data in /vault/file), so the CA survives restarts. The listener is plain HTTP on the internal portcullis network, and on 127.0.0.1:8200 on the host only. The container runs as the image's non-root vault user (100:1000).

./portcullis vault init is idempotent and is run by init, upgrade and restore. It does three things:

  1. Init, on the first run only, with one key share, threshold 1. It writes to secrets/ (dir 0700, gitignored):
    • secrets/vault-init.json: the root token and unseal key (0600)
    • secrets/vault-unseal/unseal-key: mounted read-only into the vault container. Owned by you, group 1000, 0640 (dir 0750)
  2. Unseal. After that, vault/entrypoint.sh unseals automatically on every container start: up, restart, host reboot.
  3. Least privilege for enroll. It creates the AppRole portcullis-enroll with policy vault/policies/enroll.hcl, which allows only pki_int/sign/client-cert, listing pki_int/certs and reading pki_int/cert/*. The credentials in secrets/enroll/ (group 10002 = the enroll user, 0640) are mounted read-only into enroll. Enroll logs in for 1-hour tokens and logs in again before expiry or on a 403. There is no static or root token in .env. Rotate the secret-id with ./portcullis vault rotate-enroll-secret.

The admin commands (pki setup, cert enroll|renew|revoke|list|sync, status) use the root token from secrets/vault-init.json, or VAULT_TOKEN if exported. They use the host vault CLI if it is installed, otherwise the CLI inside the vault container. The token is passed by environment-variable name, never on the command line. secrets/ and backups/ are masked from the Hub container with empty tmpfs mounts.

pki setup is idempotent and never replaces an existing CA: it only recreates missing pieces such as the client-cert role or the exported CA files. If it finds an incomplete PKI (an earlier run aborted before the intermediate was signed), it wipes and recreates it; any Vault error aborts instead of being mistaken for "no PKI". If Vault has no CA but certs/ca-chain.crt exists (Vault data lost), it refuses to create a new one. Restore a backup, or pass --force and re-enroll every certificate. See the CLI Reference.

certs/server.key is written 0640 with group 0 (Traefik runs as root but without CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE). When the CLI is not run as root, it changes group ownership through a throwaway root container (pinned alpine, only CAP_CHOWN, no network).

Trade-off of auto-unseal. The unseal key lives on the same host as the encrypted data. Root on the host, or anyone who can read secrets/, can unseal Vault. What it does protect: a copy of the vault_data volume alone is useless. Several Shamir shares on the same disk would add nothing, hence one share.
